data.Keywords Plus: REGIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; GUANGDONG-PROVINCE; POSTREFORM CHINA; ZHUJIANG DELTA; STATE POLICY; URBANIZATION; INVESTMENT; INEQUALITY; MIGRATION; GEOGRAPHY
data.text: Much of the development literature and the theory of urban transition have been based on an arbitrary division of production space into city and country side. Despite growing recognition of the need for an integrated approach to urban-rural relations, controversial issues related to the definition and measurement, of the phenomenon remain unresolved. This case study of spatial transformation in China's Pearl River Delta analyzes with greater precision the geographic extent and functional attributes of a zone of urban-rural interaction located outside and between major metropolitan centers. This zone has been the spatial focus of industrial and commercial development, although most of its population remains officially classified as agricultural. The peri-urban zone was initially left behind by the central cities in terms of its contribution to the regional economy After a decade of postreform development, this zone has moved ahead of the central cities and become the region; main destination for in-migrants and foreign investment. The growth of the zone of urban-rural interaction outside the central cities has absorbed a significant amount of the increased urban population, but it has not brought about a reduction of regional economic inequality because of the persistence of a backward economy in the periphery Theoretical questions are raised concerning the validity of several fundamental assumptions underlying the conventional model of urban transition.

Data and Methodology

Clearly, the PRD has undergone a remarkable process of accelerated economic growth and regional development. It is acknowledged that dramatic economic and spatial development in the PRD may not be typical of the general situation of the country. However, a detailed study of spatial transformation of a region that has moved 'one step ahead' of the nation may still shed important light on what may occur in other Chinese regions that have just started to experience a similar practice of economic reforms and opening up.

Data for this study were gathered through documentary research and field investigations conducted in China between 1980 and 1997. Updated information was obtained from the recent publication of national and provincial statistical yearbooks (CSSB 1996; GPSB 1996). Systematic and comparable data for quantitative analyses focus on the period of 1980 to 1990. There are two major reasons for using the 1980s data. First, choosing the 1980s as the period of study allows the utilization of economic data that are measured at the constant 1980 prices without the distortion of inflation. Second, in 1991 the provincial authorities of Guangdong conducted a comprehensive survey of county-level economic performance in the 1980s. This survey has resulted in a comprehensive data set at the county-level and on an annual basis for the years 1980-1990 (GPSB 1991). Because of the constant administrative changes that took place after 1990, the data set of the 1

Study Site

The Pearl River Delta (PRD; Fig. 1) 2 selected in this study represents a natural 'laboratory' suitable for empirical analyses to answer the questions raised above. Located on the southern coast of China's mainland, the PRD is one of the most populous and rapidly urbanizing regions in the country. A subtropical climate, fertile alluvial soils, and a water system good for year-round irrigation and transportation have made the PRD one of the largest rice bowls in China, supporting a large and dense population for centuries. The existence of large

metropolitan centers nearby, including Hong Kong and Guangzhou (the primate city of Guangdong Province), has created great market demand for the production of various farm commodities and led to the development of an agricultural system in which paddy rice cultivation and cash crops are intensely mixed. Over the years, the continued growth of farm commodities has given rise to thriving trade and manufacturing, based primarily on local agricultural produce. In turn, this has paved the way for cities and towns to flourish across the region. By the end of the nineteenth century, the PRD was already one of the most commercialized and urbanized economic regions in China, second only to the lower Yangtze (Skinner 1977, 211-249). Viewed in a geographic perspective, the conditions identified by McGee and Ginsburg in their model of urbanrural interaction appear to be

Research Scope

This study investigates the development of a spatial form of urban-rural interaction in China's Pearl River Delta. Specifically, it seeks answers for three interconnected questions: 1) Does the kind of zone of intense urban-rural interaction postulated in the Ginsburg-McGee model exist in the Chinese context, and if so can it be identified and delineated? 2) How special is this zone when compared with other spatial entities such as the central cities and the countryside, and what are its functional attributes in terms of economic production, population, and land use? 3) What is the regional effect of the emergence of this zone, and what are the implications of its growth for economic and social development at the broader regional level?

Introduction

tudies of urbanization and national development have traditionally been based on an unambiguous distinction of city and countryside. Most research has tended to treat urban and rural development as separate issues, with little consideration of the linkages and interaction between the two components (Roberts 1978; Gilbert and Gugler 1982; Harris 1982). In recent years, however, a growing number of scholars have become increasingly critical about the adequacy of the arbitrary urban/rural dichotomy (Unwin 1989; Friedmann 1996; Douglass 1998; T acoli 1998). For instance, studies of urbanization in many developing countries have revealed a distinct phenomenon of urban-rural interaction 1 that can often be found in the areas surrounding and between major metropolitan centers (Ginsburg, Koppel, and McGee 1991; McGee 1991; Potter and Unwin 1995). These regions do not fit neatly into the conventional category of 'urban' or 'rural' settlements, but they demonstrate features of both types. While the significance of urban-rural interaction in developing counS

tries has been addressed, its precise geographic extent, functional attributes, and implications for policy-making remain elusive. As several writers on the subject have openly admitted, there is considerable ambiguity concerning the measurement of urban-rural interaction and delineation of its area coverage, partly because of the lack of relevant data and partly because of the evolving

Theoretical Context

Despite its definitional difficulty, urban-rural interaction is generally understood as a process of linkages and exchange between the two loci of change in a broader context of social formation (Harvey 1985, 14-15; Unwin 1989, 12). It may take the form of the flow of people, commodities, capital, information, and other social transactions (T acoli 1998, 147; also Preston 1975; Gould 1982; Potter and Unwin 1995). It can also manifest itself in the new form of spatial complexes in which urban and rural or industrial and agricultural activities are intensely mixed or 'interlocked' (Ginsburg 1990, 31; McGee 1991, 7; Zhou 1991, 89). This study focuses on the spatial manifestation of urbanrural interaction with special reference to the development of what has been known as zones of 'urban-rural integration' ( chengxiang yitihua ) in the Chinese context.

Although there is a dearth of literature on the linkages and interactions between urban and rural areas, there exists a long tradition of scholarly interest in the relations between town and country as two different economic and social organizations. Ravenstein's (1889) 'law of migration' represents one of the earliest theoretical attempts to conceptualize the movement of people between town and country as a result of the perceived economic differences between the two loci. data.text: This article critically examines the role of food sovereignty interventions in the mitigation of the impacts of neoliberal economic policies on poor farmers in the Telengana region of India. Findings based on eighteen months of ethnographic research in the Telengana region reveal that small and poor farmers face socioeconomic and cultural constraints to the adoption of food sovereignty practices and ideals. Food sovereignty prescriptions based on localized, sustainable, and subsistence agriculture paradoxically constrained farmers' chances of maintaining viable rural livelihoods in a harsh economic climate. Este articulo examina criticamente el papel de las intervenciones de la soberania alimentaria en la mitigacion de los impactos ejercidos por politicas economicas neoliberales sobre los agricultores pobres de la region Telengana, en la India. Los hallazgos logrados con base en dieciocho meses de investigacion etnografica en esa region revelan que los agricultores pequenos y pobres tienen que enfrentar restricciones socioeconomicas y culturales para la adopcion de las practicas e ideales de la soberania alimentaria. Las prescripciones de la soberania alimentaria basada en una agricultura localizada, sostenible y de subsistencia paradojicamente restringen las oportunidades de los agricultores de mantener un sistema de vida rural viable en medio de un clima economico dificil. Basandome en estos hallazgos, sostengo que al contrario de lo que proclaman sus mentores, en el sentido de ver la soberania alimentaria como condicion previa para una genuina seguridad alimentaria, los agricultores primero deben tener comida y seguridad de medios de vida para ejercer una verdadera soberania alimentaria que les permita mayor control sobre su subsistencia.

The Telengana Context

Research was conducted among fifteen villages of the Western Medak district of the Telengana region, with two villages being the focal point of the ethnographic research. Food sovereignty interventions have been actively promoted by a nongovernmental organization (NGO), Rural Development Initiatives (RDI), in seventy-five villages in the area since the early 1990s. This research used a political ecology approach that combined a place-based study of local actors contextualized with a historical analysis of the capitalist transition of agriculture and a multiscalar treatment of food sovereignty. Methods included focus group discussions, surveys, semistructured interviews, life histories, informal discussions, and participant observation.

Secondary data in the form of land records, crop histories, and local news articles were also used.

The Telengana region (see Figure 1) forms part of a contiguous semi-arid belt and is considered 'backward' in terms of its human development (Nagaraj 2008). The region is characterized by rain-fed agriculture, poor soils, drought, and cultural and economic marginalization. Since India adopted neoliberal economic policies, already vulnerable farming systems have given way to widespread agrarian distress in the form of farmer suicides (Nagaraj 2008).

The region still primarily cultivates food crops such as sorghum, lentils, and oilseeds in nonirrigated lands and commercial crops such as sugarcane, potato, and banana in irrigated lands. Genetical

Drawing the Lines: Food Security and Food Sovereignty

The ideological basis of food sovereignty implies control and autonomy over the food system, something that is not addressed by food security paradigms. The term attained global significance after V´ ıa Campesina, a transnational peasant coalition, deployed food sovereignty to oppose the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs (GATT) as compromising the rights of nations to produce their basic foods and being inimical to the interests of peasant farmers (Edelman 2014). Since then, food sovereignty has been widely adopted, and its definition expanded, reflecting its growing appeal as a discursive weapon to protect the interests not only of small food producers but increasingly of consumers and states (Wittman, Desmarais, and Wiebe 2010).

Food sovereignty is a call to address the failings of the food security paradigm that do not address who produces the food, how food is produced, and who benefits from its production and sale (Desmarais 2007). data.Article Title: From Labor to Life in Vegetal Geography: Exploring Ontological Marginalization and Critical Externalities in the Plantationscape of a Global South Country
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: developmental paradox; existential exclusion; indigenous livelihoods; ontological marginalization; vegetal geography
data.Keywords Plus: TRIBAL POPULATION; COLONIALITY; HEALTH; SPACES; INDIA
data.text: In the ever-expanding era of urbanization where the dominance of the urban human increasingly defines global society, marginalized subaltern groups in remote rural spaces remain stark reminders of systemic inequities. Nowhere is this more evident than in India, a rising superpower whose rapid growth paradoxically coexists with deep-rooted societal divides. Within its vegetal geographies, such as the tea plantations of the Global South, landscapes of cultivation are not merely sites of production; they are living terrains where plants, labor, and social hierarchies intertwine, reinforcing the very inequities that urban progress claims to transcend. This study explores the ontological marginalization within the tea plantationscape of the Dooars region in India. Ontological marginalization is conceptualized as the systematic exclusion of marginalized ways of being, rooted in colonial histories and perpetuated by modern socioeconomic systems. The findings reveal a paradox of livelihood duality. On one hand, subsistence practices rooted in collective labor, seasonal variability in livelihoods, and reciprocal exchange continue to sustain households. On the other, these practices are increasingly enmeshed in exploitative wage economies that define the vegetal geography of tea gardens. In this landscape, the very plants that anchor livelihoods also structure social relations, tying human survival to cycles of cultivation that reproduce dependency and marginality. The research reveals how historical disruptions, contemporary structural inequalities, and gendered dimensions of exclusion have perpetuated intergenerational poverty and systemic vulnerabilities. It argues that addressing ontological marginalization demands rejecting colonial development logics and embracing justice-based frameworks that value diverse ways of being, knowing, and surviving.

Case Study, Methods, and Settings

This study is based on a cross-sectional, ethnographic investigation conducted over fifteen months, employing a mixed-methods approach at the household level. The site, also the primary field location for my doctoral research, enabled sustained engagement with the Oraon community and deeper contextual understanding. Data collection (July 2022 -September 2023) combined semistructured interviews, participant observations, case histories, and social mapping. Using purposive sampling, the Draft Electoral Roll of 2020 identified areas of high Oraon concentration in Jalpaiguri district, with Mal subdivision selected for its spatial variation and demographic density.

Mal subdivision, located in the Dooars region at the foothills of the Sikkim Himalayas, includes three community development blocks (Mal, Matiali, and Nagrakata), further divided into twenty-two Gram Panchayats (Figure 1). This population-based observational study employed both ethnographic observations and a systematic ' door to-door ' household survey, using a predesigned interview schedule. Random sampling selected 200 households per block (total 600 households; 2,909 individuals), with 487 male- and 113 female-headed households. The sample was designed using Daniel ' s (1999) formula for infinite populations, ensuring statistical robustness. Dualism in Geography of Backwardness: Equity or (In) Equality

When the government comes with promises of development, we are the ones who always lose our forests, land, and homes. Who is this development really for? (#R49, M, Grassmore TG)

The preceding quote captures the irony of pseudodevelopment, a phenomenon I observed during my doctoral field work in a rural tea garden in the Dooars region, at the foothills of the Darjeeling Himalaya. This apprehension, ' progress ' for some and ' disposability ' for others, emerged intensely through interviews and focus group discussions, which revealed among Oraon inhabitants a sense of exclusion not limited to poverty and neglect but extending to invisibility within developmental discourse: a basic absence from contexts defining modern progress (Paradies 2020). What surfaced was not only the irony of pseudo-development, where ' growth ' narratives mask deepening precarity, but also the existential ' weight of being ' relegated to the periphery of normative imaginaries of citizenship, value, and development.

In India, where blunt wealth divides reinforce social stratification and economic expansion coexists with entrenched hierarchies, development programs claiming to foster inclusivity often reproduce structural inequalities. They displace and dismantle Indigenous forms of life, disrupt relational economies, and impose extractive logics on already vulnerable communities (Byrd et al. 2018; Paradies 2020; Clendenning 2024). This is absolute in the plantationscape 3 of Dooars, where the Oraon, hi

Historical Foundations of Marginalization and Disruption of Traditional Equity Systems

Historically, Oraon social structures centered on collective labor and reciprocal exchange, fostering solidarity and equitable resource sharing. These systems were disrupted by colonial interventions and later neoliberal state policies, which formalized land ownership and replaced shared governance with private landholding (Majumder 2025a). Colonial land revenue systems (Guha 1968, 1980) prioritized extraction and surplus production, displacing the Oraon from ancestral lands and weakening mutual labor exchange, thereby introducing new stratifications. Land alienation became widespread, pushing many to forest fringes, a legacy that continues today, intersecting with postcolonial development agendas, industrial expansion, and displacement.

As one elder from Abhihill Tea Garden lamented:

The land that once sustained our ancestors now operates by others. Four generations ago, we were compelled to leave our ancestral homeland and were resettled here … laboring in the tea garden. We have spent our entire lives working relentlessly, hoping for a better livelihood, decent living conditions, and enough food for our families. Nothing has truly changed. (#R56, M, Abhihill TG)

The preceding testimonial underscores the persistent dissonance between externally imposed development models and the community ' s intrinsic rights to livelihood, identity, and territorial belonging. data.text: How researchers describe groups living within or near the world's tropical rain forests has important implications for how and why these groups are targeted for assistance by conservation and development organizations. This article explores how data about market behavior can be used to assess one aspect of forest peoples' liveihoods: their dependence on forest resources as a source of market income. With the intent the importance of methodology, to how we describe forest peoples' livelihoods, I draw from a multiyear survey of market activity among the Tawahka-nested measures of the Tawahkas' engagement in forest-product sale. Results indicate of Honduras and distinguish dicate that whether or not the Tawahka-or any forest group-can be considered financially dependent on forest resources depends on the spatial and temporal scales at which data are aggregated. As a group, the Tawahka earned 18 percent of total market income from forest-product sale, but their group profile masked a high degree of heterogeneity at the village and household level. Similarly multiyear data indicated that while group-level generalizations adhere from year to year, they belie considerable change in households' market behavior across years. I discuss three ways in which the findings are relevant to the theory and practice of conservation and development in the humid tropics. I emphasize the importance of spatial scale in interventions, how market-oriented conservation schemes can benefit from a broader conceptualization of the economic context in which forest-product sale occurs, and how longitudinal analysis can reveal the dynamism of forest peoples' livelihoods.

Study Region

The Honduran Tawahka, who numbered about 1,000 at the time of the study, are a subgroup of Mayangna, or Sumu, of whom the majority live in Nicaragua. In Honduras, the Tawahka homeland is centered along the midchannel of the Patuca River. The area straddles three Honduran departamentos (political regions) and lies at the southwestern edge of what is known as the Mosquitia region (Figure 1). Here, the pine-covered coastal plain ( < 75 m) of the Mosquitia meets the Colón and Patuca ranges, which support broadleaf rain forests that include Honduras' most endangered biota (Cruz and Benitez 1994; Harcourt and Sayer 1996).

Most Tawahka live in one of five permanent communities (subsequently referred to in this article as Villages A-E) located along a 40-km stretch of river. Most communities have consolidated around a Catholic church and school, and most Tawahka children receive three years of basic education. Communities differ in size (in 1998, Village A had a population of 624; Village E, 64) and in the area of adjacent floodplain. Only Village A had a government-funded health clinic during the 1990s.

Data and Methods

To establish a picture of the role of forestproduct sales within T awahka market production, I analyzed information about the sale of goods and services compiled from three household-level surveys: one conducted in 1995 by a research team from the Harvard Institute for International Development (HIID), and two that I conducted in 1996 and 1998. 4 I organized these data into two sets, one comprising a single year of market production (1997-1998) for about 100 Tawahka households and the other covering three years (1994, 1995, 1997) for a subset of 49 households from one T awahka village. Below, I describe how the data were collected and organized.

Defining Terms

In this study, 'financial dependency' on forest resources at any analytical scale is defined as the sustained and near-exclusive use of forest resources as a source of market income. As discussed earlier, this narrow definition of forest dependency focuses only on the contribution of forest products to a group's ability to meet its market needs, and in no way addresses the myriad other ways in which peoples living in or near tropical rainforest derive benefits from their local environment. The following describes how I distinguish dependence from the three other nested measures of which it is composed.

First, for any scale of analysis, I define participants as those who sold forest products in a given time period. I distinguish levels of participation through draw , or the total income earned from the sector (measured here in Lps). As used here, 'draw' refers only to income flow and says nothing about the actual flow of resources from the forest, although elsewhere, forest-derived income has been used to proxy for the 'market consumption' of forest resources (see Godoy and Bawa 1993). Reliance , then, refers to the share of total market earnings derived from forest-product sale (measured as a percentage). I distinguish reliance as high, low, or moderate by stratifying the sample rather than by using an absolute measure (following Coomes and Burt 2000). data.Article Title: MIGRATION PATTERNS DURING A PERIOD OF POLITICAL AND ECONOMIC SHOCKS IN THE FORMER SOVIET-UNION - A CASE-STUDY OF YAROSLAVL-OBLAST

data.text: This paper examines migration in Russia during the period that preceded the breakup of the former Soviet Union (FSU) and during the current transition period. An unusually rich dataset is used to conceptualize the impact that the political and economic collapse of a world superpower has on a migration system. A regional case study of migration in Yaroslavl' Oblast from 1989 through 1992 is used to examine the relevance of expected outcomes given standard theories of migration, empirical regularities found in capitalist economies, and past trends in the FSU. The data clearly show a migration system undergoing political and economic shocks. A significant decline of the volume of flows and a relative increase in the importance of interrepublic movement indicate disruptions. Increased relative mobility for those in the later years of the working-age population and increased importance of urban-to-rural migration flows are also important changes evident in this migration system undergoing shock.

Data and Methods

Migration data for Phase I 1 come from the annual population register data collected in Yaroslavl' by the oblast government. Register data collected at the oblast level are probably of higher quality than those presented at the national level; by the time the national level receives the data, they have passed through several government offices, each having the potential to introduce error. Trained sociologists calculated this dataset by hand using the original registry forms. Although human error can occur in the absence of computerization in

Russia, the population accounting in this dataset is the best available to date.

Several major drawbacks, however, exist due to the nature of the registry system. First, inmigration data are more accurate than outmigration data. Individuals must register as they migrate into a place in order to receive social services, including housing, education, and public assistance, but no such incentives exist to register outmigration. Outmigration data are generally underestimated, but due to the absence of place-to-place migration data, we cannot estimate the level of undercounting. Within this particular dataset, however, we can measure 6% undercounting for intraoblast migration. Second, the urban accounting systems are more accurate than the rural ones. Rural inmigration and outmigration are likely undercounted. Third, there are two separate counts of intraoblast migrat

Yaroslavl' Case Study

The Russian and Soviet migration systems have undergone shocks in the past due to major violent events such as the I917 Russian Revolution, civil war, and World War 1 1 . Characteristics of the migration system persisted despite these events-the north-to-south and west-to-east flows and rural-to-urban flows.

The essential problem here is to conceptualize how the direction and composition of migration flows within the migration system(s) of Russia may change during the post-Soviet period-a time of instability, disintegration, and reintegration, not a wartime period. There are likely to be several overlapping yet distinct phases of migration. The reality of the situation suggests that although the phases may be distinct, no one phase will be evident in isolation in any one place or at any one point in time. Phase I, destabilization, describes the late 1970s and early 1980s when the reversal of the north-to-south net exchange occurred. Phase I foreshadows Phase 1 1 , disintegration, when the chaotic patterns occasioned by the current destabilization and politicaVeconomic shocks become evident. The initial period of destabilization ended in the late 1980s just as pereswoyka was ending. Phase I1 migration should be evident in the 1990s, with 1989 being a transition year when both Phase I and Phase I1 patterns co-existed.

Soviet and Russian Case

Questions relevant to the changing direction and composition of migration flows in the Soviet and Russian context during a shock period include: What happens to the direction and composition of migration flows when a socially, economically, and politically integrated multinational state with distinct ethnic homelands breaks apart? What happens when strong government control over social and economic processes begins to fade? When, if ever, do major systemic changes occur?

The answers to these questions lie, in part, within the context of the previous migration system, one that was not well-studied by Western social scientists. Many studies of migration in the FSU successfully predict the volume and direction of migration flows using standard economic models despite the contextual problems related to the noncapitalist setting (Rybakovskiy 1973; Zaytsev 1973; Lysenko 1977; Ball and Demko 1978; Fuchs and Demko 1978; Grandstaff 1980; Maksakova 1986; Mitchneck 1990, 1991). These studies note the improvement of material welfare and quality of life as determining factors in the decision to migrate and destination choice. Standard economic models produced highly accurate predictions of the volume and direction of the flows (Grandstaff 1980; Mitchneck 1990 and 1991). Two themes emerge from these studies. First, global climate change could alter agricultural productivity, requiring adjustment of certain agricultural practices. Second, present strategies used to estimate climate impacts on agriculture have several shortcomings. Perhaps the most critical shortcoming involves accurate representation of climate change at a spatial scale where agricultural impacts are felt. Clearly, the impact of climate change over broad agricultural regions should result from the aggregated effects at local levels. Yet projecting climate change down to the local scale remains difficult. Many climate impact studies rely on general circulation model (GCM) output to provide initial estimates of climate change. Even though GCM results presently represent the most reliable and comprehensive means of estimating potential climate change, the spatial and temporal resolution of the output is typically too coarse to use directly with crop yield models at a local scale (Riebsame 1990; Rosenzweig 1990).

Most researchers have acknowledged the uncertainty associated with regional and local scale climate change scenarios and have recognized the need to present a range of potential impacts that con

Review of Migration Trends

For Western social scientists conceptualizing migration patterns in Russia, standard tools such as Ravenstein's laws of migration, life-cycle theory, the Harris-Todaro model, public choice models, and many others may be useful. These models help us to predict migration patterns according to variables such as distance, gender, age, unemployment, and local government policy. The relevancy of these traditional models, however, to non-Western, developing countries has been questioned (Brown and Sanders 1981). Approaches that relate to both less developed and more developed contexts should be considered here due to the prevalence of multiple development contexts in Russia and the USSR.

In the particular context of the disintegration of the FSU, we question the relevancy of previous work on forced refugee flows and international return migration, particularly repatriation. Most of this literature explains refugee flows during times of violent revolution or temporary labor migrations related to refugee

data.text: In 1994, support for European Union (EU) membership was highly variable across Norway, Sweden, and Finland. The ''no'' vote was strongest in rural areas eligible for substantial EU subsidies. Moreover, the majority voted against EU membership in Norway. To explain these outcomes, this article focuses on the ways in which local and national differences mediated interpretations of the issues raised during the campaign. The analysis highlights Important forces shaping northern Europe today and their implications for the EU in the years ahead.

Mediating Factors at the National Level

Norway, Sweden, and Finland have distinctive political, economic, social, and cultural attributes and, for many, these influenced how the arguments surrounding EU membership were understood and interpreted. A brief examination of the situation of each of the Nordic countries that voted on EU membership can thus provide insight into the variable successes of the 'yes' and 'no' campaigns in northern Europe.

Mediating Factors at the Local Level

Beyond national differences among Finland, Sweden, and Norway, the remarkable continuity in the internal spatial character of the EU membership vote across all three countries requires explanation. For those living in the more densely populated areas of Norway, Sweden, and Finland, the arguments in favor of membership were apparently persuasive-persuasive enough even to overcome projections that EU membership would have negative economic consequences for the larger cities of Finland, Sweden, and Norway. These arguments were clearly less effective in the rural periphery, even when combined with projections showing the rural periphery benefiting from EU subsidies. The reasons behind this outcome can be discerned from the preceding discussion. The urban areas of the Nordic countries are dominated by those who define their interests more in national terms and who therefore were more easily persuaded by the macroeconomic and political influence arguments of the 'yes' campaign. By contrast, those living in more remote rural areas were more likely to be swayed by the prospect of diminished local control and the restructuring of the rural sector.

data.Article Title: From the Right to Energy to the Right to the Countryside and Back Again: Contextualizing Rural Energy Transitions
data.Source Title: PROFESSIONAL GEOGRAPHER
data.Author Keywords: land use; populism; poverty; rural areas; sustainability transitions
data.Keywords Plus: FUEL POVERTY; POPULISM; POLITICS; AREAS; UK
data.text: Rural areas as well as their interlinkages with urban agglomerations have gained increasing attention as the main sites where the current energy transformation toward the use of renewable energy is taking place. Due to this, contestations over transitions and emancipatory efforts to transform energy infrastructures cannot be detached from the structural conditions of rural areas and their entanglements with other spatial scales. In this sense, sustainable energy transitions reflect various differences between as well as within rural areas. Consequently, rural energy transitions are embedded in broader processes of rural change. This contribution to the Focus section illustrates interconnections between energy transitions and rural change as they relate to issues of land-use change in rural areas, rural poverty, and marginalization, along with rural populism. In doing so, we argue that energy transition plays an important role for all these issues of rural development and advocate for a systematic integration of the transformation of energy systems and rural change. We, thereby, believe that contextualizing rural energy transitions can contribute to the realization of a right to the countryside and of just and sustainable rural futures within the energy sector and beyond.

Rural Energy Transitions and Rural Change

Different modes of energy provision have historically influenced rural areas and have entailed specific challenges, while also presenting opportunities for rural development. From a geographical perspective, the transition from a system based on fossil fuels toward a system predominantly based on decentral, flexible, low-carbon, and renewable energy consists of more than just substituting fuels. It involves structural changes to the energy supply, distribution, and consumption of energy, as well as a reconfiguration of related spatial patterns of economic and social activities (Bridge et al. 2013). In what follows, however, we use the term energy transitions to merely focus on transformations on the side of energy supply and its energetic sources.

Access to variable renewable energy resources like water, biomass, wind, and sun, the availability of land for the deployment of energy infrastructures, and a lower population density are main reasons why material expressions of the energy transition mostly manifest in rural areas. The focus of academic and political attention has often been on urban energy transitions, however (e.g., Cast  an Broto 2019). It is only recently that a debate about rural energy transitions has started to emerge (e.g., Clausen and Rudolph 2020; Calvert et al. 2022; Uleri, Vigan  o, and Musolino 2025). The transition toward an energy system based on renewable energy sources requires the often-contested designation and allocation of locations where new

Land-Use Change and Energy Transitions in Rural Areas

The large-scale rollout of renewable energy requires land on which infrastructures like solar and wind farms can be deployed, necessitating a far-reaching return to a horizontal surface-based energy regime in contrast to the use of subterranean fossil fuel sources (Huber and McCarthy 2017). Consequently, rural areas have gained critical attention in the energy transition, in particular, as contested resources for the deployment of renewables that undergo dual processes of revalorization and marginalization. In particular, linkages between available land resources in rural areas and renewable energy development have become the focus of critical scrutiny. Foremost in the rural context, renewables have turned into a formative element of the global land rush, green grabbing, and land deals (Scheidel and Sorman 2012).

The interrelationship of renewable energy infrastructures with rural areas remains ambiguous, however. On the one hand, the expansion of renewables has been associated in the Global North with expectations for rural economic development (e.g., Clausen and Rudolph 2020), linked to employment during the development and operation of the sites, the localization of the supply chain, increased tax revenues, and proactive benefit sharing. Regarding rural regions in the Global South, enhanced electrification and the local anchoring of the supply chain have also been highlighted as a positive. data.text: To improve geographical accessibility to health facilities in rural Ghana, it has been recommended that additional health facilities be built. Resource constraints make this recommendation infeasible. Using location-allocation models, this paper demonstrates that in the Suhum District of Ghana substantial improvements in accessibility can be achieved with better locational choices and without additional facilities. Also, additional facilities will produce little improvement in accessibility if location is not explicitly considered. The paper demonstrates the utility of location-allocation models for improving accessibility to services in the Third World.

Studv Area

The Suhum District is in the Eastern Region of Ghana (Fig. 1). It is one of 10 pioneering districts which the government of Ghana selected to implement the PHC policy in the country. Consequently, it is the focus of ongoing research into the planning and delivery of health services in Ghana. In fact, at the time of fieldwork for this research, the district was involved in a World Health Organization assisted project to delimit the catchment areas o f health facilities and identify gaps in service delivery.

According to the latest available (1 984) census, Suhum has a population of 146,100 and encompasses about 877.5 sq km (District Health Management Team 1987). The district is located on the edge of Ghana's forest belt. The district capital, Suhum, has a population of 19,298 and is 60 km from Accra, the national

Figure 1: Ghana and location of Suhum District.

capital. Suhum has several central place functions, including education, administration, commerce, and health. Besides Suhum, only Nankese has a population exceeding 3,000 people (3,414), and just 14 communities exceed 1,000. The remainder of the population is located predominantly in small rural farming villages (Fig. 2). Because of this skewed population distribution, Suhum is the hub of most activities in the district.

The district has 30 government health facilities altogether: the C-level facility at Suhum, six B-level facilities, and

Data Requirements and Modelling Approach

Essential data for this study included population and locational information for each community. Population data were obtained from the 1984 population census. Because Ghana does not have a digital spatial database, locations were digitized as x and y coordinates from the Ghana 1:50,000 map series obtained from the Ghana Geologic Survey in Accra. There were no major problems with the maps, but the population data of some smaller communities had been aggregated with larger centers close by. Another minor problem was communities with different locations but simi- lar names. These were carefully organized to avoid assigning the wrong population figure to any location. A simple distance generating algorithm was used to generate Euclidean distances between locations.

The analysis involves 150 population centers in the Suhum district as demand points and the population at each center as the proxy for demand. Euclidean distances are used because walking is the main mode o f travel in Suhum district. This avoids the problem of seasonal inaccessibility along different types of roads. The Tietz and Bart (1968) heuristic algorithm was used. The modelling approach treats the three levels of service independently and locates an optimal system of 30 facilities in keeping with the successively inclusive nature of the system. Seven of these will provide B-level services, and one of these seven will provide C-level

pMedian Accessibility to Higher-Level Services

Next, the provision of higher-level services beginning with B-level is considered. Because it is successively inclusive, seven of the 30 facilities in the actual system provide B-level services. In order to confomi to this hierarchical structure, the optimal model must select seven facilities from the 30 providing A-level services to maximize proximity to users. The results are presented in Table 2. Hodgson (1 984) demonstrated that such a bottom-up approach can result in suboptimal higher-order facilities. This effect is evaluated by selecting seven facilities freely from the open system of 1.50 demand points. This system, however, differs from the bottom-up solution by less than 1% (Table 2). The optimal p=7 system would provide an AWD of 3.28 compared to 3.7.5 in the actual system. The actual B-level system is thus not as accessible as it could be, since it involves 1. 5 % more travel distance than the p-median system. In fact, six optimally located facilities would provide an AWD of 3.6 km and involve less travel than the actual system (Table 1).

Introduction

eveloping countries face the problem of D improving their health care delivery systems but lack the necessary resources to do this. Health facilities are often geographically inaccessible to the majority of the rural population (Freund 1986; Lasker 1981; McEvers 1980; Stock 1985). Women and children, in particular, experience difficulties in reaching a source of care (Phillips 1990), but the explosion of health care costs makes it increasingly difficult to improve geographical accessibility to services. Attempts to extend care are frequently hampered by financial and human resource shortages and other barriers (Phillips 1990).

Given this problem, better spatial organization of existing health care delivery systems is a logical strategy to follow. Rushton (1984, 1988) has argued strongly for the role locationallocation models might play in using limited resources more efficiently to provide access for those currently without access. In their work in Nigeria, Ayeni et al. (1987) show that accessibility to maternal and child health clinics could be improved substantially through careful location of new facilities. Yet, critics such as Phillips (1990) question the usefulness of locationallocation models in the Third World. Phillips (1990, 145), citing the problem of data availability and reliability, states that 'optimally designed spatial health delivery systems are not practical in the Third World.' Historically, the Ghana Ministry of Health has grappled with an 'unacceptable disparity between service coverage and quality in urban areas compared with rural areas' (Adjei et al. 1984). In 1972,149 of 298 government doctors worked in the Accra-Tema metropolitan area which contained about 8% of the country's population (Sharpston 1972). In 1978, an estimated 70% of the population were unable to use the official health system (Ministry of Health 1978) because of prohibitive distances to rural facilities.

The dilemma of the Ghana Ministry of Health has been how to provide an efficient and equitable system of service throughout the country with a highly constrained budget. To accomplish this, Ghana adopted a Primary Health Care (PHC) policy in 1978 with a stated goal to 'maximize the total health of the Ghanaian people' (Mmistry of Health 1978,9). data.text: Narpes Commune, South Ostrobothnia, is the center of the largest area of greenhouse horticulture in Finland. Its presence is an example of local adjustment to agricultural decline and increased population pressure. The empirical horticultural evidence is the basis for a theory of economic transition for depressed rural areas.

A THEORY OF ECONOMIC TRANSITION

The successful evolution and development of greenhouse horticulture in Narpes illustrate a process that has been occurring in Finland and some other areas of Europe. Two excellent examples from other communes in western Finland are fur farming, centered on Jakobstad, and Konni clock manufacturing, in Ilmajoki. Each of these industries represents the adjustment of a local area to declining agricultural resources and increasing population, essentially the same conditions that once prevailed in Narpes.

An inductive theory explains the occurrence in rural areas of highly specialized industrial communities formed by similar small-scale enterprises, originally with quite low technological levels (Palomaki 1983). Thus far, empirical results have come from Finland and from central Europe. The point of departure is an older agricultural area, where all available agricultural resources have been used, so that expansion in any traditional way is no longer possible (Fig. 4). The economy is so one-dimensional that virtually no other ways of livelihood exist. Transportation is slow and expensive. No possibilities for commuting to adjacent, more developed areas exist because the process of urbanization there is still in an initial and rudimentary phase. Therefore, livelihood necessarily remains centered on the local area.

BEGINNINGS

Poverty in Finland was widespread during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when the country was part of the Russian Empire. Especially in South Ostrobothnia, evidence of the low economic status included large-scale emigration during the first quarter of the twentieth century to the United States, Canada, and Sweden (Atlas 1993, 3.9). More than half of all Finnish emigrants originated in South Ostrobothnia.

Many people who remained existed at a barely subsistence level. Farmsteads were small, even by the Finnish standards of the time, and continued subdivision of land by inheritance made agriculture increasingly less economical (Atlas 1993, 3.5). Thus conditions were opportune for a new and promising agricultural venture, however radical in approach. During the nineteenth century a few commercial greenhouses had been established around Helsinki and Turku to serve their sophisticated and affluent urban markets, but greenhouse agriculture was unknown elsewhere in Finland.

data.Article Title: FEMALE ACTIVITY SPACE IN RURAL BANGLADESH
data.Source Title: GEOGRAPHICAL REVIEW
data.Keywords Plus: WORK
data.text: Mobility and employment opportunities of women have traditionally been restricted in rural Bangladesh. As poverty increases, women in poor families seek work to support families. This trend has resulted in expansion of female activity space, after many years of stability. This article analyzes female space in the context of purdah, the patriarchal family structure, and the spatial organization of rural settlements. It discusses ethnic and other differentials that influence female space. Governmental and nongovernmental organizations are urged to create additional employment opportunities for rural women, so as to expand further their activity space.

BACKGROUND

The extent of female space in rural Bangladesh is closely linked to the purdah, which is deeply rooted in Islamic doctrines. The word literally means curtain or veil, and the practice epitomizes the exclusion of women from public male space and their seclusion in the home compound, which is surrounded and shielded by houses, foliage, and fencing (Feldman and McCarthy 1983, 949; Chen 1986, 217). Purdah is often one of several instruments of patriarchal family structure that enable men to dominate women in rural Bangladesh (Cain, Khanam, and Nahar 1979, 1). Men usually exert power and authority over women, because the former control property, income, and women's labor, and because husbands generally are five to fifteen years older than their wives. Purdah and patriarchal family structure have produced a rigid division of labor by gender and a system of social stratification that makes women extremely dependent on husbands and places them at extreme risk when husbands prove unreliable or withdraw support. The women's apparent insurance against such potential risks is children, especially sons, the birth of whom confers some status and autonomy on a young woman (Chen 1986, 217-218).

data.Article Title: SPANISH COLONIZATION AND INDIAN PROPERTY IN CENTRAL MEXICO, 1521-1620
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE ASSOCIATION OF AMERICAN GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: COLONIAL AGRICULTURE; CONGREGATION; DEPOPULATION; ENCOMIENDA; LAND GRANTS (MERCEDES); HACIENDA; INDIAN PROPERTY; MEXICO; PUEBLA; TOLUCA
data.text: After the conquest of Mexico (1519-21), the Spaniards coopted Indian administrative structures, allowing the King and the new Colonial government to exploit traditional regional revenues. Key participants of the military campaigns were rewarded with rights to the tribute and limited labor conscription (encomienda) required of the indigenous population in a particular district. Legally, encomienda did not confer property rights, but holders of the privilege also received most of the earliest land grants and had the advantage of conscript labor during the planting and harvest seasons. As the encomienda system was gradually reformed and phased out, agriculture and stockraising became the major source of rural income for increasing numbers of Spanish settlers. Public land was overwhelmingly awarded to officials, the military, and the Colonial elite. Following the failure of the Puebla experiment (1531-34), designed to create a new class of farmers with small holdings, agricultural work was relegated to Indian labor. Property became the focus of competition between Spaniard and Indian, ending with partial dispossession of Indian lands by the early 1600s. The granting of lands (mercedes) is explicated by three examples: the Basin of Mexico, the district northwest of Puebla, and the Valley of Toluca. Archival documentation of land grants provides a powerful tool to decipher regional settlement histories and to examine the degree to which the Spanish legal system safeguarded Indian properly rights. Spanish agricultural expansion was made possible by the Indian demographic collapse, as a result of recurrent epidemics, and was facilitated by Indian settlement amalgamation (congregacion). While the processes and temporal patterns of property transfer show structural similarities in the heart of Central Mexico, settlement histories in peripheral areas are unique. The means by which Indian communities slowed Spanish expansion are discussed. The pattern of dispossession of the Indian was established during the first hundred years, setting in motion a process that culminated with the powerful haciendas of the nineteenth century.

Tribute

Before 1519 the Spaniards had encountered chiefdoms (cacicazgos) with limited social organization or centralized authority on the Caribbean islands and along the Isthmus of Panama. Spanish commercial activity, beyond a little barter, had been focused on the exploitation of gold and recruiting of the necessary labor. The state organization of the Aztec empire offered more attractive possibilities, not only to seize its accumulated wealth, but to exploit the apparently unlimited flow of state revenues, to the benefit of all participants in the Conquest, from the king to the common foot-soldier. Such exploitation of tributary revenues marked the first phase of exploitation of the Aztec Empire and, a little later, its Inca counterpart.

Even before Conquest had been completed, the Spaniards had tapped considerable wealth. This included the direct spoils of war and, more important, the 'gifts' extorted from the indigenous rulers. The sealed treasury of Moctezuma and the rooms filled with gold that belonged to Atahualpa are the best known examples. Ornaments of inestimable artistic value were hurriedly melted down to gold bars. Treasures lay open for the taking. data.Article Title: The Role of Domestic Food Production in Everyday Life in Post-Soviet Ukraine
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE ASSOCIATION OF AMERICAN GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: coping tactics; domestic food production; economic marginalization; informal economies; Ukraine
data.Keywords Plus: RUSSIA; NETWORKS; RETHINKING; TRANSITION; ECONOMIES; POVERTY
data.text: The Soviet Union's collapse brought economic uncertainty to many Ukrainians. Approximately 20 percent of the population, 10 million people, currently survive on incomes below the state-set subsistence minimum figure. Given the unrealistic nature of this state-produced definition, opovertyo levels are in reality much higher. A distinctive feature of this marginalization is its longevity, as seventeen years since the dismantling of the command economy relatively few feel the benefits of marketization. As Burawoy (2001) noted, the very fact that few people have starved to death during this period indicates that other economic practices must be in operation to ensure households survive. Therefore, there is a need to explore how people (re)structure their everyday lives in response to economic marginalization. Revealing such practices demonstrates the multiplicity of forms that economic marginalization can take, the relationships between formal and informal economies, the exploitation of marginalized groups, new spaces of resistance, and the potential impact of state reforms. Although there is an emerging literature qualitatively exploring the coping tactics developed as in response to economic marginalization, there has been little qualitative examination of the role that domestically produced food plays within this broad spectrum of practices. This article begins to fill this lacuna by exploring the various roles that the dacha, a plot of rural land given to households during the Soviet period, plays in everyday life.

Overview

The coping tactics we have discussed, developed by households in response to economic marginalization, are deeply entwined within the communities and locations through which they operate and are facilitated by high levels of social capital. Contrary to Putnam's (1993) assumptions about how they are created or employed, this does not involve the membership of organizations or other civic engagements, newspaper readership, or trust in the state; rather, they are informal and rely on high levels of trust between people in similar economic situations. To return to Lefebvre, 'in short it is close to daily life,' and it is anticipated that our findings will resonate with qualitative research undertaken on informal work, everyday practices, and the development of tactics to negate economic marginalization in other locations and contexts. As Samers (2005) noted, research on informal economies often fails to consider their negative aspects. Therefore, it is important to reiterate here that the preceding arguments are not an attempt to overromanticize these coping tactics as alternatives or resistance to formal market relations or to cast them as a nostalgic 'return to the land.' Often the work is arduous, extremely time consuming, and does not allow people to save for a time when they cannot physically undertake such work. Therefore, there is a constant fear of what the long-term future will hold. The thoughts of a senior citizen from Kharkiv echoed the views of many interviewees:

Economic Marginalization and Everyday Life in the Post-Soviet Era

Although there were many negatives in the late Soviet era, there was a sense of stability. Basic foodstuffs were sometimes difficult to access, but prices and wages remained stable, allowing households to plan their economic futures. Retirees received a pension and subsidies, which, interviewees recounted, allowed an acceptable standard of living. Economic marginalization, however, came quickly to many Ukrainians following the Soviet Union's collapse. By 1993 inflation reached almost 10,000 percent per annum ( ˚ Aslund 2002), wiping out savings and drastically reducing the real worth of wages. The economic crisis engulfing the country during this period is epitomized by the fact that it was not until 1996 that the first post-Soviet bank notes could be introduced (Wilson 2005). Unsurprisingly, such turmoil saw many endure economic marginalization and by the decade's end it was estimated that 30 percent of the population had incomes below a subsistence level (World Bank 2005). Relative economic recovery saw annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth of almost 9 percent between 2001 and 2004, yet there are still high levels of economic marginalization. In late 2004, the Orange Revolution saw a change of government in Ukraine, signifying a break from the previous, allegedly corrupt, regime and a shift in political and societal outlook away from Russia toward the European Union (Wilson 2005); however, as Larrabee (2007, 46) noted, the expected outcomes from the revolution were 'cl

A Return to the Land as a Coping Tactic?

The use of tactics to negotiate everyday life is not unique to the post-Soviet period. Shortage economies in the Soviet era meant that many developed networks to access scarce products and services (Lovell, Ledeneva, and Rogachevskii 2001). The domestic growing of food was also undertaken. In response to overcrowding in urban areas, the state provided families with plots of land on which they could escape from the city and grow food if they wished (Lovell 2003). The majority of the food grown would be consumed within the family network or used as a barter currency for other goods and services and constituted a large proportion of overall agricultural production (Southworth 2006). Therefore many post-Soviet tactics have deep historical antecedents. For many, what has changed is the reason for undertaking them. Many interviewees stated that in the Soviet period they had money to buy goods but there were no goods to buy. Now there are plenty of goods to buy but they have no money to do so. Although both rationales are concerned with scarcity, the post-Soviet period has seen a dramatic increase in uncertainty. For example, workers with low incomes know they will have to continue working, either formally or informally, past their retirement age, as pensions are so low. data.Article Title: DOES LOCAL RURAL HERITAGE STILL MATTER IN A GLOBAL URBAN WORLD?
data.Source Title: GEOGRAPHICAL REVIEW
data.Author Keywords: Belgium; community; countryside; heritage; sense of place
data.text: Since 1976, the NGO Qualite Village Wallonie has worked to safeguard local rural heritage. Yet, over the years, the staff working at the NGO have noticed important changes in rural communities, including other perspectives on the local heritage. This may be linked with rapid changes in demography or changes of interests with globalization. This paper documents the apparent loss of sense of local heritage among inhabitants of the Belgian countryside and, in doing so, reflects on the sense of local places in an era of globalization. Based on interviews with the staff of the NGO and on an e-survey, the research presents a number of explanations for the findings. The results show a shift of attention away from religious and farming heritage toward places that make the village unique. The notion of heritage is evolving from something of the past that requires protection to things, sometimes intangible, that could be useful for the present and future generations. People claim that local heritage matters for the bonding and well-being of rural people.

METHODS

This research aims to support the reflection of the NGO 'Qualité Village Wallonie' (QVW). After more than 40 years of projects all over Wallonia, QVW questions both their actions and also the evolution of the sense of heritage (the current utility of local heritage and its future prospects) in suburban countryside marked by global culture. In order to support QVW in their questioning, we first conducted semistructured interviews and workshops with the staff and the administrators of QVW. Seven interviews were recorded and transcribed for analysis by both authors. Most of the people interviewed have several decades of experience in the domain and can trace people's interaction with local heritage over that time.

The insights gained from the interviews are used in conjunction with the results of an e-survey filled in by 1091 people from March to June 2020 . A web page with a URL has been created via the online tool 'framaforms' to host the survey. We restricted the number of entries per IP address to one. The questionnaire is short and playful to avoid participants abandoning it during the process. It allows people to reflect on their surroundings and their involvements in the local community. A GEOGRAPHICAL APPROACH

According to Brian Graham et al. ( 2000 ), geography and heritage intersect. First of all, heritage is a spatial phenomenon because it is embedded in space through its location, context, and spatial scale. Thus, the perception of heritage can vary according to the environment in which it is situated and the scale (local, regional, national, and international) at which we observe it. Secondly, cultural geography considers heritage as an identity component of a place and geographers are interested in studying specifically how the history of the place is expressed, particularly by the individual. Finally, heritage is considered as a resource of the territory, useful for the development and attractiveness of the territory. In this regard, heritage is a cultural and economic good to be commodified.

Looking at the French geographical literature dealing with heritage, Vincent Veschambre ( 2007 ) pointed to three periods. First, the geographers, who are more comfortable with the material world, examined particularly pragmatic issues of heritage relating to planning and local development: how to integrate heritage in the contemporary living space and how can heritage play a role in local development, especially through tourism development. During the second part of the twentieth century, rural space in Belgium, a small country ( 30 , 500 km 2 of territory and 11 . 5 million inhabitants) in the European Union with a predominantly urban population ( 91 . 5 percent) (OECD 2018 ), experienced a major decrease in the number of farmers and accommodated urban sprawl. Large sections of the population commute to cities for work, shopping, and recreation. At the same time, the rural economy experienced a diversification based on services, the primary sector, but also industrialization (Van Hecke et al. 2010 ). Concerning the demographic situation, rural space experienced, on one hand, a loss of active people and the aging of the population and, on the other hand, arrivals of commuters that led to a decline in the native population's share of the total people. THE EMERGENCE OF A LOCAL HERITAGE

In Western Europe, the 1980 s were marked by an interest in the notion of heritage, not only national heritage that makes kings and nations, but also broader expressions of heritage. After years of Americanization of European society, it has felt like a necessity to pay attention to heritage and to rediscover local and regional peculiarities. As a result of lifestyle changes, people's attention shifted toward noticing vernacular elements of their environment that they perhaps had not seen before. This leads to the emergence of new heritage, more 'banal' and 'quotidian,' but more relevant for people due to stronger attachment and symbolic meanings (Jones 2017 ; Lekakis and Dragouni 2020 ).

data.Article Title: ''Re-claiming'' land in the Gambia: Gendered property rights and environmental intervention
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE ASSOCIATION OF AMERICAN GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: land reclamation; gender agroforestry; political ecology; resource tenure; environmental intervention
data.Keywords Plus: POLITICAL ECOLOGY; STABILIZATION; CONSERVATION; TANZANIA; WOMEN
data.text: By definition, land reclamation programs render marginally productive land resources more valuable to a broader set of users. The question of who gets access to rejuvenated lands is often highly political, however. Environmental managers ''reclaim'' land resources by rehabilitating them, but they simultaneously reanimate struggles over property rights in the process, allowing specific groups of resource users to literally and figuratively ''re-claim'' the land. Relying on data gathered during fourteen months of field work between 1989 and 1995, this paper analyzes the openings created by environmental policy reforms introduced over the past two decades along The Gambia River Basin, and the tactics and strategies rural Gambians have developed to manipulate these policies for personal gain. Specifically, I demonstrate how women market gardeners pressed ''secondary'' usufruct rights to great advantage to ease the economic impact of persistent drought conditions for the better part of a decade, only to have male lineage heads and community leaders ''re-claim'' the resources in question through donor-generated agroforestry and soil and water management projects. This is thus a study of the responses different community groups have made to a shifting international development agenda centered on environmental goals. It is simultaneously an analysis of those environmental policies and practices and their impact on gendered patterns of resource access and control within a set of critical rural livelihood systems.

Three Waves of Land Reclamation

In the early 1980s, after a decade dominated by an average 25 percent shortfall in annual rainfall accumulations, rural families along The Gambia's North Bank found themselves in dire circumstances. Rice production levels were in steep decline (Kinteh 1990), imports of this principal staple were growing rapidly, and its consumer price was up sharply (Jabara 1990). The official price for imported rice doubled between 1980-1981 and 1984-1985, and more than doubled again in the four years following implementation of the national Economic Recovery Program (ERP) in 1985-1986 (Jabara 1990). The price for groundnuts (peanuts), the principal export crop produced in The Gambia River Basin, was extremely low due to negative terms of trade onthe international vegetable oils market (Jabara 1990; von Braun et al. 1990). At the same time, the effects of 'recovery' via the ERP dramatically altered production costs for groundnut growers. Between 1984 and 1987, in real terms, fertilizer prices increased 11 percent, groundnut seed nearly doubled in cost, and the price of hired labor and draft animals rose by almost a third (Johm 1990; Puetz and von Braun 1990). The net effect of these changes was severe: a sharp decline in fertilizer usage, lower earnings for groundnut producers (primarily male farmers), and a general withdrawal of labor from groundnut production, which was the source of as much as 90 percent of the country's foreign exchange throughout the period.

data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: cities; critical geopolitics; planetary urbanization; revolutions
data.Keywords Plus: CONFLICT; CITIES; STATE; CITY; GEOGRAPHIES; URBICIDE; VIOLENCE; LIFE
data.text: There has been a surge in references to urban geopolitics over the last twenty-plus years. Reviewing claims that warfare has urbanized, however, yields questions about the delineation and frontiers of the urban. The multiple meanings and definitions of geopolitics and urban beckon a broadening range of sites and an analytical deepening of urban geopolitics. To these ends, reviewing and seeking to develop the field in conceptual terms, the article revisits rural-urban interactions and reflections from selected African and Asian sites. The overall aim of the article is not to delimit urban geopolitics, but to deepen and expand agendas, broadening the range of cases that inform these. This also invites deeper geopolitical engagement with literature on extended and planetary urbanization.

Parameters of Urban Geopolitics

According to Spanu (2023) the turn to urban geopolitics means ' examining the connection between transnational geopolitical transformations, the production of space, and acts of violence at the urban scale ' (2). Describing urban geopolitics as ' a heterogeneous interdisciplinary engagement, ' Rokem and Boano (2023, 1671), noted, however, that ' generally it is not a theory-based approach -there is no ' urban geopolitical grand theory or theories '' (1672). Although chasing a grand theory might not be helpful, the stage is certainly ripe for careful examination and development of empirical and theoretical horizons.

Taking stock a few years earlier, Rokem et al. (2017) discerned two strands of urban geopolitics: work on ' militarization of urban space , surveillance and security ' and ' research … focused more specifically on urban conflicts within ethno-nationally contested cities, especially in relation to the role of planning and architecture ' (253, italics in original). Surrounding the Cities from the Countryside

Although there are other examples of nationalist and conflict discourses that invoke the rural as a reservoir of national purity and attendant sacrifice, or conversely as contamination for a cosmopolitan city, such as those described regarding the wars accompanying the collapse of Yugoslavia by Jansen (2005) and Simmons (2001), one of most significant forms of geostrategic thought on city -countryside relations was born in twentieth-century China. The notion of the countryside surrounding the cities in a conflict was developed in the context of China ' s civil war and struggle against Japanese imperialism culminating in the communist victory on the Chinese mainland and Mao ' s proclamation of the People ' s Republic in Tiananmen Square on 1 October 1949. As the British historian of China Bickers (2017) characterized it:

What was most striking about the new state was its rural foundations: a peasant revolution, led by a [former] peasant had complete control over the world ' s most populous country. No other such state existed or had existed in world history … the ' Shanghai-ization ' of China -the spread of hybrid urban culture from the coastal cities -should be countered, for it was complicit in China ' s fall and was demeaning. The ' humiliation ' visited on China by imperialism could be cleansed by the authentic, wholesome culture of rural China. (293 -94)

data.Article Title: A multilevel analysis of agricultural trade and socioeconomic inequality in rural Mozambique
data.Source Title: PROFESSIONAL GEOGRAPHER
data.Author Keywords: inequality; international trade; mixed methodologies; Mozambique
data.Keywords Plus: INCOME INEQUALITY; CLIMATE-CHANGE; LIBERALIZATION; CONTEXT; IMPACT; WINNERS; LOSERS
data.text: This study uses a mixed methodology to investigate the relationship between agricultural trade and socioeconomic inequality in Mozambique at multiple geographical scales. The quantitative analysis examines all rural regions of the country and a nationally representative sample of rural households, whereas the qualitative analysis focuses primarily on two case study villages. Research findings suggest that social and geographical context greatly influence the relationships between agricultural trade and regional inequality. Trade-related effects on economic inequality-and the social status of traders-vary across Mozambican regions. Results suggest that trade increases inequality in regions where traders have low social status, but reduces inequality in areas where they have high social status. These findings suggest that social and economic factors work together to shape landscapes of inequality.

Research Design

This study employs a mixed methodology to study both human experiences and broad regional economic trends, enabling a more comprehensive analysis of the drivers of inequality (Carvalho and White 1997; Tashakkori and Teddlie 1998; Courgeau 2003). The study was conducted between 2002 and 2004 using a sequential process in which findings at each research phase influenced data acquisition and analysis in subsequent phases (Figure 2). For example, macroanalyses informed the selection of the case study sites and local fieldwork influenced the selection of variables for the econometric models. Empirical results were verified in follow-up interviews and discussions with Mozambican farmers, allowing findings from later phases of the analysis to inform the interpretations of earlier results. Factors that cannot be easily quantified, such as social standing and community cohesion, were explored using qualitative analyses. The study can be divided into five phases.

The first phase of the study involved extensive background research and a geographic information system (GIS) analysis of social, economic, and physical factors to select a case study from among the less developed countries. Building on the methodology outlined in O'Brien et al. (2004) and O'Brien and Leichenko (2000), this study used GIS to construct poverty maps and vulnerability profiles for countries. The Case of Mozambique

Twokey factors led to the selection of Mozambique as a case study for researching linkages between inequality and agricultural trade. First, much of the debate surrounding the effects of globalization centers on how much international trade contributes to the rising levels of global and national inequality (Wood 1994; Rodrik 1997; Anderson 2005). Mozambique has an export-led economic development policy that relies on increasing regional and international trade. In-depth empirical studies on Mozambique may well lead to insights on the role international trade plays in generating social and economic inequities in emerging economies at multiple geographic levels (e.g., region, household, individual). Second, Mozambique has introduced protrade policies in an environment where the majority of the population lives in absolute poverty, people are highly vulnerable to natural hazards, and smallholder farmers make up the majority of the agricultural sector. Such poverty and vulnerability of farmers are common in the less developed countries, and therefore these factors warrant inclusion in studies of the relationship between agricultural trade and inequality.

Mozambique adopted a structural adjustment program in 1987, following a brief period of socialism and centuries of Portuguese colonial rule. The country's structural adjustment was one of several austerity programs sponsored by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) implemented in sub-Saharan Africa in the 1980s and 1990s. IMF-sp

Data Limitations

Although the use of a mixed-method, multiscalar approach enriched the scope of this study, the analysis has two main limitations. First, the use of large secondary data sources to construct the cross-sectional, regional database might have introduced error into the regression analyses and bivariate analyses depending on the accuracy of survey data. The reliability of social and economic data gathered through extensive government surveys is a common concern among social scientists, especially given the financial constraints of data collection in less developed countries. However, the variety of secondary data sources that exist for Mozambique allowed me to employ triangulation (i.e., cross-checking the calculations derived from one data set against those of another) to verify the reliability of secondary data sources. This technique indicated the robustness of key measurements derived from the available data sets and used in this study, such as mean incomes and percentages of households engaged in agricultural trade.

The second key limitation comes from the cross-sectional research design of the regression model and bivariate statistics, which prevented the study from capturing the temporal dimensions of inequality. Longitudinal studies that can control for period fixed effects (such as natural disasters) at the district level would enable an analysis of the impacts of changing trade pressures on inequality over time. data.Article Title: Chasing Moving Targets in Rural Spaces: Local Policing and Drug-Related Interventions
data.Source Title: PROFESSIONAL GEOGRAPHER
data.Author Keywords: drugs; police; rural; Sweden; time-space compression
data.Keywords Plus: POWER
data.text: Globalization in rural areas is commonly described in terms of both challenges and opportunities. Opportunities include increased communication and reduced distance. These factors, however, are also favorable for illicit activities such as increased opportunities for marketing drugs on the Internet and reduced barriers for transporting drugs. The drug industry is global and involves cross-site processes, but the drug problem is very local. This article discusses how drug activities infiltrate the work of professionals in rural places and the way this affects rural people and their living environment. In local communities, the police have the authority to counteract the spread and use of drugs, an authority that is described as geographically thinned. That is, police as well as other professionals combating the effects of drug abuse are affected as local cooperation, which is often encouraged by short distances, dense networks, and local knowledge, is weakened. Using a qualitative interview approach, this study argues that local practices related to prevention of drug-related crime are poorly equipped to deal with the speed and range of the contemporary drug trade.
