Model and Data

We fit a log-linear regression model to the casualty count of all casualty-producing tornadoes occurring in the United States between 1995 and 2016. The model is described in detail in Elsner, Fricker, and Berry (2018) and includes energy dissipation and population density as the two most important factors that statistically explain casualties. Energy dissipation (power) in units of watts is defined as the product of path area, air density, and the weighted sum of the velocity cubed. The summation is over the six possible damage ratings and the weights are the fractions of path area by damage rating. Velocities are set as the midpoint wind speed defined by the EF scale (Fricker et al. 2014; Fricker and Elsner 2015; Fricker, Elsner, and Jagger 2017; Elsner, Fricker, and Berry 2018). Population density is the number of people per square kilometer within the damage path of the tornado.

Here the model of Elsner, Fricker, and Berry (2018) is expanded to include the number of mobile homes within the path and the year of occurrence as additional fixed effects and month and hour of occurrence as random effects. Month and hour of occurrence are included as random effects to capture the cyclic change in energy at these respective time scales (Figure 1). The coefficients on month and hour of occurrence are elements of vectors of length

Definition

Knowing the physical, demographic, and environmental factors that influence casualty rates provides guidance on how to communicate the risk across a broad segment of society. For example, the regression model of Elsner, Fricker, and Berry (2018) predicts a casualty rate of twenty people (per casualty-producing tornado) for a 100- GW tornado affecting an area with a population density of 1,500 people per square kilometer. This predicted rate represents the average, or expected, count given specific values for the factors without regard to where the tornado occurs. Local, place-based factors are also important, however, in mitigating or amplifying casualty rates. To locate places where local factors might be particularly important, we examine the residuals from a regression model and define an unusually devastating tornado (UDT) as one where the observed number of casualties substantially exceeds the predicted rate.

More formally, let CT be the observed casualty count for tornado T and ^ CT be the predicted casualty rate for the same tornado from a regression model f involving known tornado-level factors X T (e.g., population density, energy dissipation, number of mobile homes, etc.). We then define a UDT as one in which the difference between CT and ^ CT exceeds some large value ( L ) (see Equation 1).

Factors Related to the Number of Casualties

Tornadoes kill and injure nearly 1,000 people, on average, in the United States each year. Previous research has identified physical factors that affect the rate of tornado casualties. These include the maximum damage rating (Fujita/Enhanced Fujita [F/EF] scale), the tornado damage path length, and the strength, or energy dissipation, of the tornado. For example, Ashley (2007) found that tornadoes categorized with a high maximum damage rating (F scale) produce the vast majority of tornado fatalities, and Fricker, Elsner, Mesev, and Jagger (2017) showed that tornadoes with a high maximum damage rating (EF scale) represent a disproportionate number of casualty-producing tornadoes relative to the total number of tornadoes. In addition, Simmons and Sutter (2005, 2008, 2009) and Lim et al. (2017) found that as tornado damage path length increases, so does the number of tornado casualties. Quantitatively, Fricker, Elsner, and Jagger (2017) noted that a doubling of tornado strength, represented as an estimate of energy dissipation, leads to a 33 percent increase in the rate of tornado casualties.

Previous research has also identified a number of socioeconomic and demographic factors that affect the rate of tornado casualties. These include the number of people in harm ' s way, the type of housing stock present (permanent or mobile), and the age and income of the population within the damage path. data.Article Title: Crip Theory and Country Boys: Masculinity, Dis/Ability, and Place in Rural Southeast Kansas
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: critical disability studies; health geography; masculinity; rural geography
data.Keywords Plus: SOCIAL MODEL; GEOGRAPHIES; DISABILITY; POLITICS; HETEROSEXUALITY; GENDER; MEN; TRANSFORMATION; PATRIARCHIES; EMBODIMENT
data.text: This article examines the discursive and material practices of rural masculinity in Southeast Kansas by fore-grounding ability and place as essential in understanding gender. It draws on empirical data gathered from autoethnographic participant-observer research conducted in the region. I begin with a synopsis of critical studies on masculinity in the field of human geography and proceed by offering a summary of research specifically addressing rural masculinities. I then illustrate contrasting perspectives surrounding dis/ability as a concept and also provide an in-depth overview of crip theory. I next describe the research context and methods utilized during the project, as well as how men use their bodies as conduits through which cultural norms pertaining to manhood are expressed, affirmed, and reproduced. My results demonstrate how situated assertions of masculinity are inextricably linked to ability, (hetero) sexuality, and sociospatial context, as well as how the pervasive yet veiled pressures of heteronormativity and compulsory able-bodiedness and able-mindedness impose banal and strictly policed social boundaries in regard to belonging and inclusion. The piece is thus a cripping of hegemonic notions of manhood in rural Southeast Kansas suggesting that both ability and place are necessary constituent elements for any critical analysis of masculinity.

'There's No (Liminal) Place Like Home': Methods and Positionality

To revisit the cultural politics of masculinity in Southeast Kansas, as well as get a sense of the broader social relations of the region, I moved 'home' to rural Kansas to live in the field for nearly ten months. For the project, I took up employment as a farmhand and traveled across several counties to speak with men about their day-to-day lives, as well as get a sense of their perspectives on masculinity, ability, and bodily practice. In total, I conducted sixty in-depth, semistructured interviews, held eight focus groups (each with five informants), and kept field notes during my daily work, leisure activities, and social outings. To initially recruit informants, I discussed the project with friends and family and asked them to spread the word among their acquaintances. I also posted flyers in local businesses, in post offices, and on community bulletin boards expressing an interest in interviewing community members who identified as 'men,' were 'from the country,' and would be willing to participate in research being conducted on 'masculinity and place.' 5

Participants who volunteered for the project were all United States citizens between the ages of eighteen and seventy-seven who self-identified as 'American,' 'male/men,' 'heterosexual/straight,' and 'working or middle class.' Of the sixty participants interviewed, fifty-four were 'white/Caucasian,' four were 'Latino/ Mexican,' and two were 'black/African American.' The homogeneity of the sample reflects the predomina

'God, Family, Country': A Social Geography of Rural Southeast Kansas

In discussing the cultural landscape of Southeast Kansas, it seems fitting to begin with two of the most noticeable, yet ordinary aspects of the region's social geography: whiteness and religion. On traveling around the countryside and while conducting interviews within differing towns it became quite clear, via both the optics and discourses, that two of the most powerful influences in the area are Christian values and nationalistic American pride. Critical research on the rural United States shows that conservative Christian perspectives have the tendency to heavily inform what politics individuals have, what moral codes they deem acceptable, and even how they behave (Wald and Calhoun-Brown 2014). This was reflected numerous times in my research, as many of the participants noted, 'If Jesus were alive, he'd vote Republican.' What regularly followed this statement were heteronormative assertions explaining that 'being gay was a cross to bear,' there is nothing 'more sacred than (nuclear) family,' and 'God made Adam and Evenot Adam and Steve.'

Further to these declarations, one fifty-two-year-old participant named Rick offered his cultural overview of the area by characterizing it as

nothing but fields and farms, with an occasional outpost that has the three things all good American towns should have: a church, a bar, and a fried chicken joint-and the church should be Catholic, and the beer cold [ laughs ].

Masculinities and Place, in Geography

Connell's (2005) neo-Gramscian analysis of gender notes that masculinities are pluralistic, defining them as 'configurations of practice structured by gendered relations' influenced by 'bodily experience, personality, and culture' (44). In expanding on the elements of power, consent, and hierarchy woven into social formations of masculinity, Connell put forth the notion of 'hegemonic masculinity,' which constitutes the practices denoting the most acceptable ways of engendering 'manhood.' Connell's thoughts on hegemonic masculinity have reshaped understandings of gender by signifying not only that multiple forms of masculinity exist but that among these variations certain ideals associated with 'being a man' are granted ascendancy over others. Masculinities can therefore be more precisely theorized as being socially policed and legitimized, internally regulated, and in constant states of flux. It should also be pointed out that fully embodying hegemonic masculinity is impossible due to the fact that 'masculinity' itself is an illusory construct functioning in a perpetual state of redefinition and instability.

More recently, Connell and other gender theorists note that in addition to being fluid, masculinities are contextualized and constituted by the places in which they are operating (Connell and Messerschmidt 2005; Mac an Ghaill 2006; Hopkins and Noble 2009). Notably, on arriving in rural Southeast Kansas I encountered these place-centric dynamics quite regularly with parti

Situating Dis/Ability and Crip Theory

Disabled people comprise one of the most diverse and active social groups in the world (Gabel and Peters 2004; Peters, Gabel, and Symeonidou 2009). Despite this, they remain one of the most acutely marginalized heterogeneous groups, facing oppression on personal, cultural, and institutional levels of society (Park, Radford, and Vickers 1998; R. Butler and Parr 1999; J. L. Davis 2006; Mullaly 2010). Oppression on the personal level can take the form of sympathy, irritation, discomfort, and annoyance as expressed by enabled 4 people in the face of those they deem to be disabled. At the cultural level, oppressions for disabled people are made manifest through disparaging stereotypes, hurtful attempts at humor, or omissions from popular culture altogether. Institutionally, oppression is evidenced by the de facto segregation, discrimination, and inequality found within the political, social, and economic systems of a society (Park, Radford, and Vickers 1998; F. K. Campbell 2009). Research has shown that these structural injustices are due in part to the entrenchment of the medical model of disability, which negatively labels disabilities as 'flaws' or 'defects' (Garland-Thomson 2002). The primary demeaning aspect of the medical model is that it locates 'dysfunction' within individuals, thereby erasing the sociospatial and systemic processes largely responsible for creating the hardships experienced by those who are disabled.

data.Article Title: US Farm Policy as Fraught Populism: Tracing the Scalar Tensions of Nationalist Agricultural Governance
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: agrarian crisis; Farm Bill; Farm Bureau; surplus; US agricultural history
data.Keywords Plus: BUREAU FEDERATION; FOOD SECURITY; CONTRADICTIONS; PERSPECTIVE; CHALLENGES
data.text: The scalar tensions of nationalism manifest acutely in agriculture-particularly in the contemporary United States. This is paradoxical because farm policy calls for and enacts nativist governance that undermines the conditions of farming: from labor to water, topsoil, and pollinators, to export markets. At the heart of these scalar contradictions is the fraught, shifting terrain of agrarian populism. The intertwined origin of the U.S. Farm Bill, the American Farm Bureau Federation, and Cooperative Agricultural Extension shows how early twentieth-century fraught agrarian populism drove farm policy but how it also carried a pivotal consensus of recognition about the ecological and economic dangers of overproduction. Drawing on archival research at the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) National Agricultural Library Special Collections, discourse and policy analysis of U.S. Farm Bills, and qualitative research with farmer organizations, this article traces how racialized xenophobia accentuates the hypocrisy of U.S. agriculture's extreme dependency on migrant labor, as heightened borders also reveal their ecological farce in the face of intrinsically transnational climate change, soil erosion, and water constraints. The America First trade agenda decries imports while sidelining the crisis of commodity crop glut and the spatial fix of subsidizing exports as surplus disposal. Yet, even amidst the scalar contradictions of nativist agricultural governance and the fraught farm populism driving it, there existed a kernel of agrarian populism grounded in a collective honest recognition of the ecological, economic, rural, and social crises of overproduction-and that organized against it. This kernel catalyzed the origin of both the Farm Bill and the Farm Bureau but has been subsumed in and through both since.

Current Fraught Agrarian Populism

The term populism remains slippery, with its increasingly divergent array of political valences. It animates all ends of political spectrums, either promoting or derailing democracy, decentralizing or centralizing power. The very vagueness of the term contributes to its potency, from authoritatianism (Scoones et al. 2018) to emancipatory potential (Laclau 2005). Amidst this wide, bumpy terrain stands agrarian populism, with its turn-of-the-twentieth century origins farmer uprisings against agro-capitalism -a democratic counter (Gilbert 2015) to liberalism, finance capitalism, and communism (Goodwyn 1978). I describe the term and realm of agrarian populism as fraught , both in the sense of being overloaded by the weight of projections and associations -many ominous -and in the sense of causing or being affected by tensions and anxiety.

At the heart of these tensions and anxiety I argue is agrarian inviability -the inability to secure a dignified livelihood and life from agriculture on a community level. The article traces this inability to the overlooked role of surplus, which has long served as a mechanism of agricultural exploitation and accumulation, a driver of scalar fixes and thus contradictions. Amidst the layers of coloniality, classism, racism, and gender hierarchies at play in U.S. farm policy, there has been a long-standing, although now muffled, conscientious recognition of the crises of commodity crop surpluses. This recognition served as a catalyst for a kernel

Fraught Populist Origins of the Farm Bill and Farm Bureau

World War I catalyzed both the U.S. Farm Bill and the Farm AFBF. Agricultural production served internal nation-building and geopolitical nation-flexing but required local, county-by-county incentivization. With European farmers in the trenches, the U.S. government aggressively encouraged farmers to expand wheat production for export to Europe. A few years of unusually high rainfall in the otherwise arid Midwest -along with advances in machinery -led to a boom in farmland expansion. Growers tilled up the deep-rooted native prairie grass to plant wheat in what would come to be known as ' The Great Plow-Up. ' As prices increased, farmers expanded their fields and new farmers moved westward to join the boom. By the late 1910s, however, European wheat production had rebounded, causing the world market to glut and prices to fall. Prices collapsed by 1920. For a decade, farmers responded by further expanding production, desperate to recoup investments. The U.S. stock market crashed, the Great Depression began, and the real aridity of the southern Midwest returned -but in extreme form. A devastating drought swept the region with prices still nearing nothing, hurling farmers into destitution and desperate migration.

data.Article Title: Race, Space, and Electric Power: Jim Crow and the 1934 North Carolina Rural Electrification Survey
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: American south; biopower; energopower; infrastructure; race
data.Keywords Plus: POLITICS; STATE; NUMBERS; PLACE
data.text: Some scholars have recently put forward the concept of energopower-the harnessing of electricity and fuel-as a way to rethink the energetic basis of biopower. In this article, I refine this idea by tracing the use of race in rural electrification planning in North Carolina during the New Deal 1930s. Drawing on archival fieldwork that examines and reconstructs the 1934 North Carolina Rural Electrification Survey, I chart the ways in which race was used to readjust and reshape projections of electricity consumption and the planning of electricity distribution line construction. This is particularly clear in the use of a metric called the correction factor that allowed electricity planners to negotiate the contradictions between the materiality of networked electricity service, based on connections, and the prevailing attitudes toward race, which were built around disconnection. Although the overall influence of the 1934 Survey on the location of electricity distribution in North Carolina remains an open question, this work highlights the ways an energopolitical project-rural electrification-intersects with a key biopolitical technology-state racism, thus providing a better understanding of the relationship between energy and social power.

The 1934 North Carolina Rural Electrification Survey

In 1932, only 3.2 percent of North Carolina farms had electricity. Rural leaders in North Carolina viewed this as a problem. By the early 1930s federal figures such as Morris Cooke (who would later head the federal REA), national and state agricultural leaders, and electrical equipment manufacturers such as General Electric (Brown 1980; Field 1990) were agitating for a federal rural electrification program, although these efforts were met with opposition from local private power interests (Manganiello 2015). For its chief boosters, rural electrification meant a restoration of a country life on par with those in cities (Phillips 2007). Clamoring for rural electrification would culminate in the formation of the federal REA in 1935, which began loaning money to build rural distribution lines in 1936. North Carolina's program actually began earlier, when in May 1934 North Carolina's governor formed a Rural Electrification Committee to coordinate the electrification efforts of existing privately and municipally owned electric utilities. The Committee's first order of business was to conduct a statewide survey to assess where rural electrification was most feasible (Brown 1982).

Few figures were more important to the 1934 survey and subsequent rural electrification efforts than David S. Weaver, professor of agricultural engineering at North Carolina State University. Weaver's academic career was largely devoted to increasing farm mechanization and he would serve as a consulting en

The Correction Factor

Twenty-four of the twenty-six household-level variables collected in the 1934 survey were based on relatively straightforward criteria (see Table 3 for an overview of surveyed households). For instance, surveyors could easily assess the number of rooms in a house, and the surveyed households could answer frankly about their desire for an iron or electric oven. Two variables stand out, however, as particularly subjective, as the survey required surveyors to make two judgments about each household.

First, surveyors were instructed to make an assessment of the condition of the house. As guidance, the instructions to surveyors stated:

By the use of the letters A, B, C, and D give a rating for the premises with the idea in mind-is the person interviewed sincere in his statements as to what he or she intends to do and do appearances point to the fact that he or she is financially able to live up to his or her promises. Race, Space, and Governance in 1930s Edgecombe County, North Carolina

The racial political economy of 1930s Edgecombe County was indicative of many counties in eastern North Carolina, home to some of the largest antebellum cotton plantations in the state. The legacy of slavery left Edgecombe as one of ten counties (out of 100 in North Carolina) with a majority African American population despite the significant outmigration of African Americans after the Civil War. Around two thirds of Edgecombe County's population of 47,894 in 1930 were classified as rural, with a vast majority of those (88 percent) employed in the agricultural sector (Table 1). Like North Carolina as a whole, the majority of farms operating in Edgecombe County were of modest size-between twenty and forty-nine acres 1 due to the prevalence of tenant farming. Tenants oversaw most farms (84 percent), acreage (73 percent), and farm value (70 percent) in Edgecombe County (U.S. Census 1930). Similar to antebellum plantations, major rural landowners in Edgecombe County performed little labor, instead acting as a rentier class that skimmed or swindled the profits derived from often African American tenant labor (Billings 1979; Woods 1998). Biopolitics and Energopolitics

Scholars have recently argued that energy has not been adequately factored into social theory. Urry (2014, 3), for example, pointed out that energy's 'varied forms structure the social, temporal and spatial organization of societies and of 'life' itself,' yet he also asserted that studies of the extent to which energy has powered society are underexamined. In a review of contemporary energy geography research, Huber (2015) called for energy to be viewed as more than an empirical object of inquiry and instead an underlying concept in our social and material infrastructures.

One area in which social theories are becoming energized is in and around Marx's investigations into the operations of capitalism. Although acknowledging the immense explanatory power Marx's work has had, recent scholarship critiques Marx for treating energy simply as any other input into a capitalist system (Labban 2008; Huber 2009, 2013a, 2013b; Szeman 2014). The treatment of energy as a raw material consumed in production processes ignores that the development of modern capitalism was deeply dependent on the exploitation of fossil fuels. Researchers are beginning to push beyond this superficial account to analyze the role of fossilized energy in producing capitalism's distinct spatialities. data.text: This article provides a visual analysis of a set of peopleless photographs taken in 2006 of a falling home erosion in the village of Shishmaref, Alaska, that have been widely circulated in reporting about the relocation of the village due to climate change. It asks whether the visual contract between spectator and absent climate change victim extends beyond an empathetic response to action toward restoring the lost home. The article explores the relationship of contemporary scholarship on postmodern ruination in U.S. Rust Belt cities and the Shishmaref fallen home photograph as a means to analyze the work done by rural ruination.

Understanding Shishmaref: Physical Positioning the Falling House Photograph

The village of Shishmaref is located on a barrier island, Sarichef Island, in the Chukchi Sea roughly five miles from mainland Alaska. It is separated by a lagoon and lies within the Bering Land Bridge National Preserve and has been inhabited for at least 500 years (Marino 2015). The population of Shishmaref is roughly 600 people and is mainly Inupiat Native Alaskan. Erosion is nothing new for Shishmaref. The land on which the village thrives is part of a dynamic barrier island chain. Residents have noted land lost to the sea from natural trends for hundreds of years -it is an impermanent and ever-changing landscape. For most of its history, though, the community ' s mobility throughout the year was also dynamic and seasonally patterned. Their movement and building of camps was flexible, and was made dependent on an analysis of weather and ice conditions. This high amount of mobility proves a successful adaptation strategy to protect the community against flooding and erosion, as movement off of Sarichef Island could be done quickly and efficiently (Marino 2015). In the mid-twentieth century, however, as a federally funded school was built on Sarichef Island, the community of Shishmaref consolidated more permanently to adhere to the mandated attendance policy. This eroded the flexibility of the community, replacing it with immobile infrastructure, often prefabricated further south and shipped north.

The Visualization of Climate Change

Shishmaref ' s visual narrative of the consequences of climate change does not exist in a vacuum. As noted in an early seminal work in the field by O ' Neill and Smith (2014), ' Visual images are everywhere in the portrayal of climate change ' (73). In surveying scholarship on the visualization of climate change in newspapers, television, and film, O ' Neill and Smith (2014) surmised that studies conducted in Canada, the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom ' find that climate change depicts identifiable people (often politicians, but also scientists, citizens, business leaders, and celebrities), the causes of climate change (such as throughout iconic images of ' smockstakes ' ), climate impacts at home and abroad, and graphical or scientific representations of climate change ' (O ' Neill and Smith 2014, 73; O ' Neill 2013). These same studies have found that images of people dominate coverage of climate change of those media outlets surveyed. In DiFrancesco and Young ' s (2011) study of Canadian print media, 66 percent of all images included people. Much of this photojournalism focuses on identifiable people, including politicians, celebrities, and business leaders. data.Article Title: A LiDAR-Based Analysis of Stream Channel Cross Section Change Across an Urban-Rural Land-Use Boundary
data.Source Title: PROFESSIONAL GEOGRAPHER
data.Author Keywords: channel capacity; channel enlargement; LiDAR; urban stream
data.Keywords Plus: URBANIZATION; IMPACTS
data.text: Little is known about the downstream propagation of stream channel alterations initiated by urban flow regimes. In this study, freely available Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) data were combined with ground survey data to derive information on changes in stream cross sections in a North Carolina watershed, moving downstream across an urban-to-rural land-use boundary. Regression analyses relating LiDAR model and ground survey data exhibit poor relationships for all channel morphometric measurements except reach-average channel capacity. Application of the channel capacity regression reveals a negative power function pattern of downstream decline in channel enlargement. The largest declines occur before streams enter the rural landscape, with more gradual declines afterward. The largest declines in channel size might be attributable to reservoir effects along reaches with wide floodplains. Model results indicate no discernible enlargement once rural land covers and percentage impervious areas of about 60 percent and 16 percent of watershed area, respectively, are reached.

Methods

Field Surveys

Ground surveys using meter tape and leveling (Abney or theodolite) were conducted to acquire data on the dimensions of twenty-six channel cross sections from ten different stream reaches (one to five cross sections per reach, spaced 20-30 m apart) along NBC and one cross section at one reach downstream of the NBC-SBC junction (Figure 1). Surveys were conducted over a period of three years from 2005 to 2008. Sites were chosen to avoid the spatially immediate effects of tributary junctions, bridges, and culverts. Bankfull elevation heights were estimated at each site using morphological criteria, including the top of well-developed point bars and prominent benches (when present) and, more commonly in the absence of such indicators, the elevation of the apparent floodplain (top of lowest bank; Harrelson, Rawlins, and Potyondy 1994). Morphological evidence of bankfull stage was emphasized due to the unreliability of features like temporary scour lines and vegetation zones along eastern streams (Harman 2000; Doll et al. 2002; U.S. Department of Agriculture 2003). Bankfull stages thus identified were judged on the basis of gauging data and postflood field evidence to be reached by flows typically occurring every one to two years, the most common frequency cited for bankfull flows in eastern U.S. streams. Bankfull channel capacity, width, and depth were calculated from the field data for each section.

Field Area

North and South Buffalo creeks head in Greensboro, North Carolina (population 250,000; Figures 1 and 2), a medium-sized city in the Piedmont physiographic province. The area falls within the humid subtropical climate zone, with an average annual temperature of 14.5 ◦ C and an average annual rainfall of 1,074 mm. Vegetation consists predominantly of mixed deciduous and coniferous trees. Upland soils are formed in residuum from metamorphosed felsic rocks and contain a clay-rich Bt (argillic) horizon. North and South Buffalo creeks (henceforth, NBC and SBC) exit the urban boundary at drainage areas of approximately 65 and 75 km 2 , respectively, and join in rural eastern Guilford County to form Buffalo Creek (total drainage area of 230 km 2 ). Total relief in the watershed is 76 m. The majority of the municipal area within the NBC and SBC

catchments has been fully urbanized since the 1960s and 1970s, respectively; thus, there has been some time for a new quasi-equilibrium state under urban conditions to be achieved.

Data on stream bankfull cross-sectional area (capacity), width, and depth for large numbers of both rural and urban streams in the North Carolina Piedmont demonstrate that urban streams typically exhibit an increase in channel dimensions relative to ru

Topographic Measurements from LiDAR

LiDAR technology allows the rapid remote acquisition of highly accurate elevation points at high spatial resolution. Expected horizontal and vertical root mean square errors are frequently less than 1 m and point spacing of refined data sets is commonly less than 4 m (Kraus and Pfeifer 1998; Baltsavias 1999; Hodgson et al. 2003). Several important limitations of LiDAR exist, though. For example, even at 4-m resolution, LiDAR returns might be ill-suited to defining features with precise boundaries such as the tops and bottoms of stream banks, necessitating manual input of breakline data derived from other sources (Maune 2001). Automated methods for filtering buildings from bare-earth surfaces tend to also filter or smooth natural features with similarly sharp topographic breaks (Kraus and Pfeifer 1998; Maune 2001; Bowen and Waltermire 2002; James, Watson, and Hansen 2007). LiDAR returns from water features are generally unreliable, due to the absorption and scattering of pulses (Maune 2001; H¨ ofle et al. 2009). In densely vegetated areas, a nearvertical pulse is needed to effectively penetrate canopy and generate a true bare-earth return (Kraus and Pfeifer 1998; Hodgson et al. 2003). The mean distance to the nearest LiDAR point might be closely tied to land cover class, with the greatest point spacing in deciduous, mixed, and scrub or shrub environments (Hodgson et al. 2003).

Morphometric Analyses with LiDAR

Despite the limitations, useful geomorphological analyses have been conducted using LiDAR data. An early application of LiDAR technology involved the measurement of channel and gully morphology. Ritchie et al. (1994) made rough estimates of river channel widths and depths by connecting minimum elevation measurements with straight and curvilinear lines using 'best judgment' practices. Bowen and Waltermire (2002) sought to identify the types of river corridor terrain most commonly associated with the largest measurement errors in the Western United States. Large LiDAR elevation overestimations were found to be common in areas with both dense vegetation and steep banks. Charlton, Large, and Fuller (2003) evaluated the abilities of LiDAR to map a gravel-bed wandering stream in the United Kingdom and found that error was introduced by both the presence of vegetation and by deep water, which tended to produce gaps in the point spacing. James, Watson, and Hansen (2007) used LiDAR to map gully networks and headwater streams under forest canopy in South Carolina. Their model captured the location of gully networks accurately but not gully channel dimensions. Overestimation of channel width and underestimation of channel depth were tied to point spacing. The authors recommended the incorporation of ancillary data such as breaklines to explicitly delineate the rims and bottoms of channels.

Urban Stream Syndrome and Downstream Hydraulic Geometry

Urban stream syndrome refers to a set of hydrological, geomorphological, and biological symptoms commonly associated with streams where a significant portion of the contributing upland catchment has been affected by urbanization (Paul and Meyer 2001; Walsh et al. 2005). As urbanization takes place in a watershed, increases in the areal extent and connectedness of impervious surfaces and the concentration of storm flow by physical conduits like sewer systems increase the volume and velocity of flow in channels (Dunne and Leopold 1978; Booth 1991; Schueler 1995). The hydrogeomorphic consequences of this include 'flashier' hydrographs with higher discharge peaks and altered channel morphology (Booth 1991; Paul and Meyer 2001; Walsh et al. 2005). data.Article Title: Finding a Disappearing Nontimber Forest Resource: Using Grounded Visualization to Explore Urbanization Impacts on Sweetgrass Basketmaking in Greater Mt. Pleasant, South Carolina
data.Source Title: PROFESSIONAL GEOGRAPHER

data.Keywords Plus: POLITICAL ECOLOGY; RURAL GENTRIFICATION; GIS; GEOGRAPHIES; MANAGEMENT; LANDSCAPE; ECOSYSTEM; AMERICA
data.text: Despite growing interest in urbanization and its social and ecological impacts on formerly rural areas, empirical research remains limited. Extant studies largely focus either on issues of social exclusion and enclosure or ecological change. This article uses the case of sweetgrass basketmaking in Mt. Pleasant, South Carolina, to explore the implications of urbanization, including gentrification, for the distribution and accessibility of sweetgrass, an economically important nontimber forest product (NTFP) for historically African American communities, in this rapidly growing area. We explore the usefulness of grounded visualization for research efforts that are examining the existence of fringe ecologies associated with NTFP. Our findings highlight the importance of integrated qualitative and quantitative analyses for revealing the complex social and ecological changes that accompany both urbanization and rural gentrification.

Case Study and Methodology

Sweetgrass, as noted earlier, is a key natural and signature resource used in basketmaking, which, according to popular discourse, is being destroyed by rapid residential and commercial development (Hunt 2006). Baskets sewn by enslaved Africans were once essential to the rice economy that helped fuel the early growth of Charleston and its rural surroundings (Pollitzer 1999; Carney 2001). By the end of the twentieth century, despite the disappearance of rice production almost a century earlier, the descendents of these slaves and their hand-built stands had become a regular site along U.S. Highway 17 in the Mt. Pleasant area and in key tourist areas in peninsular Charleston. Basketmaking remains an important part of the household economies of many African Americans (Derby 1980; Coakley 2006) in the settlements that were once rural outposts of a then smalltown Mt. Pleasant (today referred to as the 'Old village'; Figure 2 inset). What was once a small town has become South Carolina's fifth largest city and one of the state's fastest growing cities (U.S. Census 2000), complete with numerous upscale gated communities, some with golf courses and waterfront parcels with private docks. Residential subdivisions increasingly surround historic rural settlements and, in at least one case, largely have replaced an entire community, leaving only a few small pockets of homes with land-use patterns that are more rural in character and that are mainly invisible to passersby (see Figure 3 ins

Ethnography

Our ethnographic methods rely primarily on semistructured in-depth interviews, document analysis, participant observation, field research, and attendance at key community events. Our results present data from interviews conducted during June 2002 and January 2003 that were collected for an initial study that examined basket makers' views of and roles in past and current sweetgrass management (Hart 2003; Hart, Halfacre, and Burke 2004), interviews in the summer of 2003 about collecting strategies, and data from an ongoing study that specifically examines basket maker responses to urbanization. The 2002-2003 study included a total of twenty-three Charleston area basket makers (sixty were invited to participate), including basket makers from the three main locations in the Charleston area (see Hart, Halfacre, and Burke 2004 for complete details). The summer 2003 interviews included fifteen respondents from the same locations, and the 2006 data collection efforts included interviews with twenty-six basket makers (out of eighty-four who were invited to participate) from the same three sales locations as well as a newer sale site at the local farmer's market (located at Marion Square in downtown Charleston). In all three studies, participants were identified using both convenience and snowball sampling, with most identified specifically through field excursions to basket stands and additional interviews coming from referrals by participants. A variety of other ethnographic data als

GIS

To explore the intersection of ecological and social change resulting from residential growth in the area and the implications for basketmaking, we created a series of maps that provide information on (1) the distribution of sweetgrass using both the botanical literature and information provided by basket makers themselves, which provides some baseline information on areas that have been accessible in the past; (2) land development trends in Charleston County since the South Carolina colony was founded, highlighting the relationship of recent development and parcels that allow access to deep water and spectacular views; (3) land development trends and changes in the boundaries of African American communities in the greater Mt. Pleasant area, which allows us to explore the socioeconomic demographics of the incorporated and the unincorporated portions of the Mt. Pleasant area; and (4) a model of suitability and accessibility that is derived from information about environmental conditions associated with habitat suitability, land ownership, and parcel sizes that suggest the likelihood that sweetgrass on a given parcel would be accessible for collection. On the face of it, the GIS component of our analysis might be seen as merely corroborating the stories told by basket makers. Yet, it is important in a rigorous critical GIS to seek correspondence between empirical observations made by researchers, key informants, and GIS data. data.Keywords Plus: DRINKING-WATER; ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE; SECURITY; IMMIGRATION; COLONIAS; QUALITY; ACCESS; DISPARITIES; DIMENSIONS; DISTRESS
data.text: This article examines household-level characteristics that predict water insecurity in low-income rural and periurban communities on the Texas-Mexico border. We employ two logistic regression models (binary and ordered) to identify household characteristics that are more likely to result in water insecurity. Our analyses yielded unexpected findings: Whereas socioeconomic factors are weak predictors, immigration status of household members is a significant variable that contributes to household water insecurity. Policymakers need to pay more attention to marginalized communities as universal water access still leaves populations without adequate, reliable, and affordable water in the Global North.

Household Surveys

Qualitative research was conducted in Hidalgo County during nine visits between January 2009 and August 2011. The fi rst author led a research team, including a local community health worker ( promotora ), as they conducted forty-one semistructured interviews and two focus groups. The fi rst author used qualitative information to develop a household water security survey, which was then completed for seventy-one households in Hidalgo County (sixty-eight households used in study) in July 2012. The second author conducted sixty-six household surveys in El Paso County and Do ~ na Ana County (New Mexico) in July 2013. We used the State of Texas colonia classi fi cation system to stratify our sample of households (Parcher and Humberson 2009). We selected households in eleven different colonias in eastern Hidalgo County and fourteen different colonias in eastern El Paso, with households representing each colonia classi fi cation: red, yellow, green, and unclassi fi ed (Table 2). We also surveyed colonias not classi fi ed in the Texas database. We removed six household surveys from adjacent counties in New Mexico when we ran the logistic regression models to limit our analysis to Texas counties. The surveys were conducted in Spanish or English with the available head of household. The survey, which took between thirty and forty- fi ve minutes, was divided into four parts: (1) household demographics (age, occupation, health care access, country of origin, etc., for each household mem

Data Analysis

We analyzed household survey data using three techniques. First, we used an experiential scalogram technique (Guttman 1945) to draw inferences about a latent variable (water insecurity) in the observed data (Guttman 1945; Guest 2000). In this study we created three scalograms for each dimension of water security. Guttman scalograms provide a measurement of cumulative or progressive objective, subjective, and biocultural experiences; it has been particularly useful when related to domestic water access and food security (Wutich and Ragsdale 2008; Hadley and Wutich 2009; Stevenson et al. 2012). For Hidalgo County, we used household scales and classi fi cations from previously published data (Jepson 2014), and we followed the same procedure to create the water security scales and classi fi cation for households in El Paso.

Survey item responses were entered 0 or 1 into a respondent-by-item matrix for each dimension of water security, with each row representing a household respondent and each column representing an indicator for each dimension of water security (water access, water quality acceptability, water distress). Guttman scalograms order item responses such that the individual who responded more positively will rank higher than an individual who responded negatively, and the positions of the item responses and individuals are given numerical values. Three conventional measures of reliability for each scale were calculated: coef fi cient of reproducibility (CR), coef fi c

Binary Logistic Regression

Table 7 summarizes the outcome and explanatory variables used in the regression models. Table 8 presents the results from the logistic regression model for household water insecurity. Overall the model is reasonably strong as indicated by the likelihood ratio chi-square value, which is statistically signi fi cant ( p < 0.05).

Household immigration status is an important factor to consider in household water insecurity. The analysis indicates that ' mixed status ' households were 4.2 times more likely to be water insecure than households with members who were all documented (legal residents or U.S. citizens). Households in which all members are unauthorized residents increase the likelihood (1.2 times) of water insecurity, but the results were insigni fi cant. Birthplace, which is different than legal status, also signi fi cantly affected household water insecurity. Households with both U.S.- and foreignborn members are 20 percent less likely to be water insecure than households in which all members were born in the United States.

Other socioeconomic variables such as size of household increase the likelihood of household water insecurity, but the results are all insigni fi cant. Poverty level runs in the direction anticipated. Households between 50 percent and 99 percent of the FPL are almost twice as likely to be water insecure than those above the FPL, and the households below 49 percent of the FPL are 1.5 times more likely to be water insecure than those above the FPL

Household Water Insecurity Along the U.S.-Mexico Border

The waterscape on the Texas -Mexico border is de fi ned by complex hydrosocial interactions among institutions, organizations, and technologies that allocate the fl ow of water across the region and through infrastructure to different water users (Jepson 2012; Jepson and Brannstrom 2015). Rio Grande water eventually fi nds its way to poor households through circuits of irrigation-district canals, quasi-public community water networks, inadequate household connections, water vending machines, and garden hoses to be stored in fi fty-gallon barrels, buckets, or fi ve-gallon plastic bottles. A fragmented regime of water governance institutions, water markets, housing codes, and private corporations direct the water fl ow to households in border colonias. The focus of this study is two of the poorest regions in the United States: (1) Hidalgo County in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, with the largest concentration of colonias (over 240,000 people), and (2) El Paso County in West Texas (Figure 1). data.Article Title: Settin' the woods on fire: Rural incendiarism as protest
data.Source Title: GEOGRAPHICAL REVIEW
data.Author Keywords: fire; land tenure; peasant revolt; political ecology
data.Keywords Plus: ARSON
data.text: Fire is a fundamental tool within a broad spectrum of vegetation-management strategies, from swidden agriculture to plantation forestry. Through the seemingly pyromanic activity of incendiarism, fire assumes additional significance in the human-environment relationship. Case studies from England, Algeria, and the southern United States serve to illustrate the circumstance of fire as an indication of agrarian discontent and a weapon of peasant resistance. Other documented cases of incendiarism reveal that use of fire in the landscape has expanded from a constructive ecosystem-manipulation technique to a destructive form of protest undertaken by the oppressed or disempowered.

FORMS OF INCENDIARISM

An incendiary fire has been defined as a "wildfire willfully set by anyone to burn, or to spread to, vegetation or property not owned or controlled by him, and without consent of the owner or his agent" (Forest Service 1978, 9). Although the popular Hank Williams song used "settin' the woods on fire" merely as a metaphor, these illuminating lyrics are clearly indicative of actions familiar to many rural residents. Motives for such actions include personal grievances against landowners, attempts to devalue property for speculative economic gain, incidents of arson by unemployed firefighters who seek work, and the pyromanic activities of demented individuals. The focus of this article is on incendiarism as a tool of protest or resistance.

Arson is listed by James C. Scott as one of the "weapons of the weak" that "relatively powerless groups" utilize against ",those who seek to extract labor, food, taxes, rents, and interest from them" (1985, 29). Rural incendiarism, according to George

Rude, belongs "to that shadowy realm between crime and protest where it is often no easy matter to tell the two apart" (1978, 4). In cultural-ecological terms, destructive burning of the landscape represents seemingly maladaptive behavior, as a result of which the perpetrators themselves become victims. A GLOBAL ASSESSMENT

Incendiarism as a tool of protest or resistance has been a recurring, albeit sporadic, phenomenon across the globe, although certain areas are more prone to experience this activity than are others (Figure 5). A sampling of documented cases reveals the following situations, beginning with several locations once subsumed within the British Empire.

During the 1920S, in Kenya, the encroachment of European colonists into areas of traditional pasture for tribal livestock led to a government-sponsored program known as kifagio, a Swahili word for "broom," referring to the sweeping away of native stock. Resistance to kifagio included acts of incendiarism, involving settlers' crops and the forest reserves in which indigenous people were forced to relocate. The ensuing poverty led to militancy, and "acts of terrorism against settlers and their property increased," part of a peasant movement that found ultimate expression in the Mau Mau rebellion (Kanogo 1987,140). To the south, in neighboring Tanganyika during the 195os, a mandatory government soil-conservation program that included a ban on burning elicited an incendiary response: "Ribbons of smoke rose defiantly all over the Uluguru Mountains.... Rules against burning were no longer enforceable, and the peasants now openly flaunted authority by firing the hills" (Young and Fosbrooke 1960, 157).

data.Article Title: Challenges and Opportunities for Coping with the Smart Divide in Rural America
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: broadband; digital divide; ICT; rural; smart divide
data.Keywords Plus: BROAD-BAND; DIGITAL DIVIDE; BIG DATA; CITY; COMMUNITIES; NETWORKS; PARADIGM; INTERNET; CITIES
data.text: Recent success in the many applications of information and communications technologies (ICTs) in urban settings largely defines our understanding of sustainable development in the context of smart societies and communities. The footprints of such smart transformation barely imprint in the countryside, however, where rural communities face tremendous barriers, such as the absence of ICT infrastructure, geographic isolation from technological advances, and various social inequalities. The conventional wisdom of smart societies and communities built on well-established broadband access and ICT applications in urban hubs might not be suitable for decentralized rural regions. We contend that a new form of digital divide in the context of recent ICT advancement-a smart divide-is evolving into a new challenge to smart societies and communities. This study aims to characterize the smart divide, an emerging type of social inequality. To address this aim, we conduct a literature review with a focus on the technological aspects of the smart divide in rural regions and identify potential gaps in smart infrastructure and smart applications and services between urban and rural America. The article culminates in a synthesis of potential strategies for bridging the smart divide in rural America. The study is expected to benefit scientists, planners, entrepreneurs, and policymakers interested in smart rural development.

What Is the Smart Divide?

The term smart divide was coined by Lee (2016), who defined the term as a qualitative divide determined by the intellectual and skill gap within groups of smart device users. In this context, varying levels of adoption of smart devices contribute to the division among people. A subsequent paper (Nam and Park 2017) used a similar concept and definition with case studies to examine adoption differences among disadvantaged individuals. The authors viewed the smart divide as the latest evolvement from the digital divide with close ties to the digital literacy of people in association with variable income, race, gender, age, and geographic locations (Nam and Park 2017). We found that this definition of the smart divide largely aligns with similar demographic and socioeconomic dimensions of the digital divide; that is, digital inequalities, which have been well elaborated in the literature (Van Deursen and Van Dijk 2014; Shelton, Zook, and Wiig 2015; Friemel 2016; Leszczynski 2016; Kitchin, Cardullo, and Feliciantonio 2019). The rise of SCCs, however, requires the deployment of more advanced, networked, and functional ICT infrastructure, as well as the associated SASs, which are beyond the traditional technological domain of the digital divide. This profound smart ICT advancement could potentially bring the smart divide to our communities. The traditional definition of the digital divide does not fully reflect the technological contexts of progressing ICT in the age of SCCs. Our di

Technological Foundation of the Smart Divide

SCCs have evolved during the development of mutually reinforcing ICT infrastructure (Damiani, Kowalczyk, and Parr 2017) and SASs (Neirotti et al. 2014; Alaa et al. 2017). The advances in ICT infrastructure enable new SASs to be adopted and applied. Our need for SASs drives further deployment and expansion of ICT infrastructure. Figure 1 shows the overall architecture of smart ICT infrastructure and SASs in SCCs. Although both foundations (particularly the ICT infrastructure) are not brand new in comparison with their counterparts in the digital age, they present new challenges in terms of capability and penetration issues. In the following subsections, we detail the foundations and then present their link to the smart divide.

data.Article Title: Biodiversity and land-use change in the American Mountain West
data.Source Title: GEOGRAPHICAL REVIEW
data.Author Keywords: biodiversity; exurban development; land use; ranching
data.Keywords Plus: BREEDING BIRDS; COMMUNITY; URBANIZATION; PRINCIPLES; PREDATION; HABITAT; TUCSON; DEER
data.text: Rural private lands in the Mountain West of the United States are undergoing a profound land-use conversion, from agriculture to low-density residential or exurban development, though little scientific study documents the ecological consequences of this change. Nongovernmental conservation organizations are working with ranchers to keep rangeland out of development and in ranching, ostensibly because these organizations believe that biodiversity is better protected on ranches than on exurban developments. We compared plant and wildlife communities across the principal rural land uses in the Mountain West: protection, livestock ranching, and exurban development. Native plant and faunal biodiversity was better maintained on ranches and protected areas than on exurban developments. Exurban developments favored species that were nonnative or adapted to human-altered environments. The continued conversion of ranches to exurban development suggests a long-term alteration of the region's natural heritage.

STUDY AREA AND SITE SELECTION

We conducted our study from May through August during 2000 and 2001 in the foothills along the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains in northern Larimer County, Colorado (40050' N, 105°15' W). The study area is approximately 40 kilometers northwest of Fort Collins, the nearest metropolitan area. The land-use matrix of the region is a blend of private ranchland, public protected areas, and exurban developments. The vegetation is a mosaic of shrubsteppe and mixed-grass prairie. Dominant grasses include needle-and-thread (Stipa comata Trin. & Rupr. var. comata), blue grama (Bouteloua gracilis [Kunth] Lag. var. gracilis), western wheatgrass (Elymus smithii [Rydb.] Gould), and cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum L.). Shrubs include mountain mahogany (Cercocarpus montanus Raf. var. montanus), skunkbrush sumac (Rhus trilobata Nutt. var. trilobata), and bitterbrush (Purshia tridentata [Pursh] DC.). Common forbs include fringed sage (Artemesia frigida Willd.) and hairy goldaster (Heterotheca villosa [Pursh] Shinners var. villosa). Average annual precipitation ranges from 33 to 46 centimeters, with 75 percent of it falling between April and September (Moreland 1980).

The study was restricted to sites with similar physical characteristics, including the same shrubsteppe plant community, with elevations between 1,740 to 2,200 meters, and similar soil types to reduce na

STUDY DESIGN AND DATA COLLECTION

We compared songbird, mammalian carnivore, and plant communities across three land uses: public protected areas (Colorado Division of Wildlife's State Wildlife Areas) whose principal use was outdoor recreation and wildlife protection (no grazing, logging, mining, or water development); private-land livestock ranches with cattle; and exurban developments with one house per 14-20 hectares. We randomly selected ninety-three points across the three land uses to survey songbirds and mammalian carnivores and sixty-nine points to sample the plant community.1 At each point we sampled communities using 75-meter fixed-radius point counts for songbirds,2 scent stations for mammalian carnivores,3 and 20-by-50-centimeter quadrats for plants.4

EXURBANIZATION OF THE MOUNTAIN WEST

The Mountain West of the United States is experiencing a human population boom that rivals any in its history. Of the eight states that make up this region-Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming-five are the fastest growing in the country (Figure i). Metropolitan areas and their suburbs have accommodated much of this in-migration, but rural areas are growing at a faster rate (Heimlich and Anderson 2001). Driven by a mixture of economic and qualityof-life features, people are increasingly drawn to the rural Mountain West (Power 1996). Unlike previous booms driven by resource extraction and commodity production, the present period of growth is fueled by the expansion of service, recreation, and information industries and is marked by the conversion of private land use from agriculture to exurban development (Riebsame, Gosnell, and Theobald 1996; Sullins and others 2002).

As a result, three of the principal land uses in the rural Mountain West today are protection, livestock ranching, and exurban development. Exurban development refers to low-density residential development that occurs beyond incorporated city limits (Nelson and Dueker 1990; Knight 1999). The main human use in protected areas is outdoor recreation and the protection of perceived natural values; on ranches it is livestock production; in exurb

CONSERVATION RESPONSE

Concern about the conversion of the Mountain West's natural heritage from a mixture of generalist and specialist species to a narrower suite of human-adapted species has generated a new response to biodiversity protection among nongovernmental conservation organizations (NGOS). The traditional response to protect biodiversity from anthropogenic degradation has been to purchase land and designate it as a protected area. The emerging response is to work with ranchers to protect biodiversity while keeping the land in private ownership and as a working ranch (Alexander and Propst 2002). Typically, development rights on the ranches are acquired through purchased conservation easements while ranchers continue to raise livestock. This approach has become increasingly popular, especially among NGOS such as The Nature Conservancy and the Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation (Weeks 2002). In Colorado, about 35,000 hectares of private land have been protected through conservation easements by The Nature Conservancy and 24,000 hectares by the Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation (GCOFR 2000). This strategy has increased the number of land trusts that seek to protect private land in agriculture from development. By 2000, more than 1,200 land trusts in the United States had protected roughly 1,051,000 hectares through conservation easements (LTA 2001).

data.Article Title: Countryside recreational access in the United States: A statistical comparison of rural districts
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE ASSOCIATION OF AMERICAN GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: access; countryside; landowners; public; recreation; United States
data.Keywords Plus: PRIVATE LANDS; PUBLIC-ACCESS; COLORADO; IMPACT
data.text: This comparative study employs the concept of physical rigor to map and measure recreational routes and zones available to the public. The comparison is made for 20 representative countryside districts in five regional settings (Northeast, Midwest, South, Great Plains, and California). Five of the districts are national parks, while the rest are 40 x 25 km settled areas chosen to typify landscapes of their region. Statistical measures of access availability are derived from 1:24,000 topographic maps for five levels of access rigor. Access was determined for small quadrats (500 m square) on a presence/absence basis, beginning with the easiest access mode (passive) and then testing for increasingly rigorous modes (casual, vigorous, rugged, arduous, and closed). Polynomial regressions show strong relationships between levels of access and the independent variables of topography, land cover, road density (a surrogate for land-use intensity), and natural vegetation. In highly utilized areas of low relief there is plentiful access via the road network, but few trails, and much closed land. By contrast, remote wilderness areas, exemplified by national parks, offer little road access, but provide ubiquitous cross-country access for a small minority of specialized or expert recreationists. Regional variations in access availability are also tentatively related to the scale of original landholdings, in turn related both to date of settlement and type of land allotment and survey. For given levels of land-use intensity, areas of large-scale landholdings have fewer public rights-of-way, and more land closed to the public.

The Study Areas: Selection and Appraisal

The only feasible way of measuring access availability nationwide is through the use of topographic maps combined with field verification. Since the great bulk of recreational activity takes place in the settled or semi-settled countryside, our interest focuses on these areas. More specifically, the study areas selected are located in regions having continuous blocks of ecumene with rural densities exceeding t w o people per square kilometer (as shown in Figure 1) (Espenshade and Morrison 1986:86). Extensive areas of desert, mountain, and northern forest are excluded from study, as are regions containing only small pockets of scattered settlement.

To facilitate analysis and permit comparison with other studies, the United States was divided into five regions differentiated with respect to their natural vegetation, dates of settlement, and culture. The five units range in size from 100,000 to 500,000 square km, and their boundaries are drawn through thinly populated areas or along major rivers (Figure 1). Within each region, three representative settled areas were selected, each being 1,000 square kilometers in area (40 km by 25 km). The study areas met three criteria; they are: 1) largely rural with a few tracts of urban or suburban development; 2) mixed in topography, water features, land cover, and settlement types, while accentuating features typical of the local setting; a

Weighted Index of Access Availability

The potential for access is of little use if few people wish to take advantage of it. In this sense, the more rigorous modes of access are less 'available' to the general public than are easier and more leisurely modes. To weight supply by potential demand, the percentage of counters at each level of access rigor is multiplied by an estimate of the proportion of the public willing to participate at that level. Based on conceptual considerations (Millward 1991 ; Figure 2) and empirical evidence (e.g., Glyptis 1991 :I 06-1 21; Simmons 1975:26-29), these weights are set at 1.0 (passive), 0.5 (casual), 0.25 (vigorous), 0.1 (rugged), and 0.02 (arduous). Closed lands are weighted at zero, though it is recognized that they may host more recreational activity (through trespass) than do remote areas with legal but arduous access. Summing for each quadrat the weighted percentages in each mode yields a single index of access availability which ranges from zero to one hundred.

Weighted availability indices averaged for each district, park, and region appear in Table 2. They confirm many of the points already noted. Note that access availability is high in the intensively settled Northeast and Midwest (averages of 67 and 57, respectively) belowaverage in the more thinly settled areas of the Plains and California (41 and 46), and intermediate (52) in the South (which is similar to the national average of 53 for settled

Access Supply, Land Ownership, and Land Value

In a recent paper, the author outlined a conceptual framework which positioned recreational access in a broad spectrum of environmental and cultural settings and suggested measures of access supply suitable for statistical analysis (Millward 1991). The concepts and measures were applied to 13 Canadian countryside districts (Millward 1992) and 15 West European districts (Millward 1993); in each study regional variations in the quality and quantity of public access were identified and related to intensity of land use, amplitude of relief, the type of natural vegetation, and the history of land settlement and survey. This paper on recreational access in the United States complements these earlier surveys. Given the

size and diversity of the United States, regional variations in recreational access provision are expected to be considerable; older and more densely settled regions such as the Northeast should resemble the West European (and parsettled lands in the West should have more in com- ticularly British) case, while recently mon with areas of western Canada.

Recreational access is supplied or provided wherever the public may freely use routes or zones for recreational movement (Cloke and Park 1985:334). The amount supplied is related t o the geographic extent of opportunities for recreation, irrespective of the degree of utilization. Access routes include roads (paved and unpaved), tracks, paths, and w

Access Routes

The network of public roads and tracks allows physical and visual entry into the countryside even when adjacent lands are barred. For many motorists, a "trip in the country" is a leisure pursuit in i t s own right (Patmore 1974:7-71; 1987). Access is increased in areas of high agricultural value, because such areas require a dense network of exploitation roads-most of which become public rights-ofway. Access is also affected by the scale of original landholdings: an area with smaller landholdings has a finer cadastral mesh which requires more public roads. Landholding size is often related in turn to the period of settlement and to the character of earlier farming systems. The shape of original landholdings also affects the subsequent availability of public access routes: in formal land survey systems, compact parcels require denser road networks than do long lots of the same size, particularly when the latter are ranged in double-front fashion (Thrower 1966). Irregular surveys (metes and bounds) also tend to have lower road densities. Even where subsequent farm enlargement and/or farmland abandonment reduces the economic justification for a dense road network, rights-of-way are likely to remain as residual elements in the landscape, and hence as routes of access for public recreational use.

data.Article Title: They Will Destroy Themselves Wanting Purely American: Labor and Carceral Immigration Enforcement in the US Pacific Northwest
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: carceral geography; deportation; immigration enforcement; migrant labor; race and labor
data.Keywords Plus: DEPORTABILITY; ILLEGALITY; REGIMES; RACE
data.text: This article examines the upheaval associated with the extension of carceral immigration enforcement into a particular rural county in Washington State. Migrant workers in shellfish, cranberry, and tourism industries began to leave the county, either through the forced mobility of deportation or quasi-voluntarily, to rejoin deported family or to avoid deportation. This process simultaneously constrained the agency of undocumented workers and presented employers with a destabilized race and labor regime that they represented as a labor shortage. In this situation, the local race and labor regime was destabilized, to the detriment of local capitals. This article extends the understanding of the regulation of labor via carceral immigration enforcement, arguing for an understanding of the place-specific and conjunctural nature of the articulation of immigration control and labor regimes. Such an approach reveals how immigration enforcement's many functions, including the sovereignty-producing and political capital-producing functions, can work in contradiction with the labor regulating, social control functions.

Methods

For this study, I conducted a rich case study of a particular place undergoing a shift in the intensity of immigration enforcement. To trace the multiscalar complex of forces that together constitute a (changing) place, I juxtapose and weave together a broad set of sources. I draw on twenty-one key informant interviews, ethnographic field work, and archival analysis conducted in Autumn 2017, Winter 2018, Summer 2018, and Winter 2019. This is a subset of the research I conducted for my dissertation that examines detention and carceral immigration enforcement in Washington State, with extensive research conducted in and around the Northwest Detention Center (NWDC) in Tacoma.

I selected key informants who could provide expert information on the process of ICE enforcement in Pacific County and its impact from a wide variety of subject positions. I conducted interviews with county residents including three ICE targets, five family members of ICE targets, four employers, four agricultural industry experts, one local journalist, four school district representatives, four advocates, and two social service providers. In some cases, people held overlapping roles; for example, as an employer of migrant workers and a school district employee, or the family member of a target and a social service provider. I met my first informants from Pacific County outside the detention center, where they attended a rally in August 2017. These were advocates who were organizing material support for pe

Migrant Workers in Pacific County

In Pacific County, shellfish and cranberry farming, shellfish processing, and tourism together make up the vast majority of nongovernment jobs. Many Latinx workers in Pacific County work in the shellfish industry, planting, harvesting and processing oysters, mussels, crabs, and clams. They also work on cranberry farms and in the restaurant kitchens and hotels. According to the 2010 U.S. Census, the overall population of the county hovers around 21,000; in 2010, 87.4 percent of residents were White and 8 percent were ' Hispanic ' or Latinx. 3 Latinx adults, almost all from Mexico, began coming to the region about thirty years ago, and more and more began to settle, some coming up directly from Mexico and others after first living in California or in eastern Washington. Additionally, there are Latinx seasonal workers who regularly circulate through the county during peak shellfish processing season after the berry and tree fruit seasons in other areas of Washington end. The region was understood to be a relatively safe and quiet place to live and work without permits or official documentation -shellfish jobs especially paid a living wage, and Latinx residents encouraged their family members and friends to come join them in Pacific County. Informants shared with me how settlement patterns shifted over the years. In the 1990s and into the 2000s, Mexican-origin men circulated between Pacific County and various communities in Mexico, working for several years up north and then retu

Place, Articulation, and Labor Regimes

My article extends scholarship on the intersection of labor control and immigration control by theorizing this complexity through a conceptualization of place, articulation, and conjuncture in local labor regimes. Jonas (1996) coined the term local labor control regime , which he defined as ' an historically contingent and territorially embedded set of mechanisms which co-ordinate the time-space reciprocities between production, work, consumption and labour reproduction within a local labour market ' (325). This concept encompasses how local labor markets are regulated not only at the point of production, but also in the spaces of consumption and reproduction. That is, labor control extends through spatial configurations that encompass workers ' home, recreation, schooling, and consumption sites. Numerous ethnographers studying undocumented labor in rural areas of the United States in the twenty-first century have highlighted how undocumented agricultural workers manage their vulnerability to immigration enforcement by limiting their mobility, remaining close to their homes and workplaces, and maintaining their invisibility in landscapes of consumption (Nelson, Trautman, and Nelson 2015; Maldonado, Licona, and Hendricks 2016; Mares 2019). Hypervisibility to immigration enforcement officers and invisibility in the community (Licona and Maldonado 2014) marginalizes their presence in the rural landscape, affecting food access, health care access, everyday mobilities, and the cre

Immigration Control and Labor Regulation

Scholarship on precarious immigration status and migrant labor has tended to emphasize how vulnerability to immigration enforcement marginalizes migrant workers, rendering them exploitable. Qualitatively, the threats of arrest, detention, and deportation have been particularly important levers of power of employers over noncitizen workers. People with precarious or no legal status can lack access to labor protections. They are then susceptible to abusive workplace relations, and to employer retaliation for workplace self-advocacy or organizing via reporting workers ' unauthorized presence to the state (Cho and Smith 2013). Carceral immigration enforcement ' s regulation of labor can also work less directly, though. Immigration enforcement is thought to complement the needs of employers by forging a distinction between citizen and noncitizen workers (Bauder 2006; Sharma 2012) and thereby regulating the labor supply. For De Genova (2010), the spectacles of bordering, detaining, and deporting cover over social relations in which illegalized migrant labor is made both ubiquitous and subordinate. data.Article Title: Geospatial information technology, rural resource development, and future geographies
data.Source Title: ANNALS OF THE ASSOCIATION OF AMERICAN GEOGRAPHERS
data.Author Keywords: geospatial information technology; remote sensing; geographic information science (GIScience); rural systems; human-environmental interactions; geographic management systems (GMSs)
data.Keywords Plus: GIS
data.text: Geospatial information technologies, particularly as they relate to remote sensing and geographic information science (GIScience) are providing new perspectives for understanding rural systems. By utilizing geospatial technologies with more integrative research approaches, geographers can ask more socially relevant and innovative questions about the human-environmental system. Within remote sensing alone, there has been a significant leap forward in usable sensor systems for analyzing human dimensions of rural areas through high spatial and spectral resolution approaches. The impact of various forcing factors (e. g., water availability) in Kansas and Botswana, for example, within the context of human-environmental interactions can be more fully understood using such geospatial technology approaches. At the same time, through new infospheres, cybergeography, and sensitivity to new attitudes in learning by millinneals, future geographies are created that demand more geographic management systems (GMSs). At the center of such evolving trends, geographers are poised to provide important leadership in more fully understanding the human-environmental system as we begin the Association of American Geographers' next century.
